sentences.en: 哈哈
sentences.fr: 哈哈

words.notes: Chinese characters representing laughter (哈哈, pinyin: hāhā). This is a transcription artifact — likely auto-captioned laughter. In Korean, laughter is typically written as ㅋㅋ or 하하.

sentences.en: It's a ghost
sentences.fr: C'est un fantôme

words.notes: Sino-Korean word (鬼神). Commonly used in everyday Korean for 'ghost.' Also used figuratively for someone uncannily skilled (e.g., 귀신같이 알다). Here used playfully as a self-introduction — Hwasa is joking that she appeared suddenly like a ghost.

합쇼체 (formal polite) speech level. 이다 conjugated as 입니다 after a consonant-final noun (귀신 ends in ㄴ). Used here for humorous dramatic effect — the overly formal register contrasts with the playful content.

grammar.meaning: Copula 'to be' in formal polite declarative form: 'It is N'

sentences.en: I can do it
sentences.fr: je peux le faire

words.definition: To do (modifying the following noun 수)
words.notes: Future/prospective adnominal form of 하다. The ending ~(으)ㄹ turns a verb into a modifier for the following noun. Here it modifies the bound noun 수.
A dependent noun that cannot stand alone — always preceded by a verb modifier. Used in the core pattern ~(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다 to express ability or possibility.
해요체 (polite informal) conjugation of 있다. Combined with ~(으)ㄹ 수 to complete the 'can do' construction.

grammar.meaning: Can do, be able to — expresses ability or possibility

sentences.en: I do
sentences.fr: Je fais

words.notes: Contracted form of 저는. 저 is the humble first-person pronoun (vs. casual 나). The contraction 전 is extremely common in spoken Korean. Interesting register mix: 저 (polite pronoun) with a 반말 ending (그래).

words.root: 그렇다 (to be so, to do so)
words.definition: I do (that way) / That's how it is for me
words.notes: 반말 (casual) form of 그렇다. This is a ㅎ-irregular adjective: the ㅎ drops before a vowel ending (그렇 + 아 → 그래). Used to affirm or agree with something previously mentioned.

grammar.meaning: Spoken contraction of 저는 ('as for me')
Adjectives with stems ending in ㅎ drop the ㅎ before vowel endings

sentences.en: do
sentences.fr: faire

words.notes: 해요체 (polite informal) conjugation of 하다. 하 + 여 contracts to 해. This is the most foundational Korean verb. Here used as a brief confirmation or continuation of the previous utterance, switching back to polite register.

grammar.meaning: Polite informal speech level ending — the default 'safe' politeness for everyday conversation

sentences.en: rod
sentences.fr: tige

words.notes: This appears to be either English code-switching or a transcription/captioning error. It may be a mishearing of a Korean utterance by the auto-caption system. Context suggests it is not a meaningful part of the conversation.

sentences.ko: 이따가 또 뭐 미팅 얘기할 게 있어서 이건 전화가 오면 바로 또 끊어지거든?
sentences.en: I have another meeting to talk about later. As soon as I get a call, it hangs up again, right?
sentences.fr: J'ai une autre réunion dont je dois parler plus tard. Dès que je reçois un appel, il raccroche, non ?

words.notes: Time adverb referring to a short future time span, typically within the same day. Very common in spoken Korean. Sometimes shortened to 이따 in casual speech.
One of the most common Korean adverbs. Appears twice in this sentence — first meaning 'also/in addition' (another meeting), second meaning 'again' (gets disconnected again).
Contracted form of 무엇. Here used as a casual filler/hedge word (like English 'like' or 'well'), softening the statement rather than asking a question. Extremely common in natural spoken Korean.
Konglish loanword from English 'meeting.' Note: in Korean, 미팅 can also refer to a group blind date in some contexts, but here it clearly means a work meeting/discussion.
얘기 is a colloquial contraction of 이야기 (story/conversation). 얘기하다 = to talk/discuss. The ~ㄹ ending creates a prospective modifier: '(something) to talk about.'
Contracted spoken form of 것이. Very common in colloquial Korean. 얘기할 게 있어서 = 'because there's something to talk about.'

words.definition: Because there is / since I have
words.notes: ~아/어서 is a causal/sequential connective meaning 'because' or 'and so.' Here it provides the reason: 'because I have something to discuss.'
Contracted form of 이것은. Refers to the current live broadcast. Common spoken contraction in the same family as 그건 (그것은), 저건 (저것은).
전화 (Sino-Korean 電話) = phone/phone call. 가 is the subject particle used after vowel-ending nouns. 전화가 오다 = 'a call comes in' — the standard expression for receiving a call.
~(으)면 is the conditional ending meaning 'if' or 'when.' No 으 needed since 오 ends in a vowel.
Common adverb meaning 'immediately,' 'directly,' or 'right (away).' Emphasizes how quickly the disconnection happens.

words.root: 끊어지다 (to be cut off, to get disconnected)
words.notes: 끊다 (to cut, to hang up) + ~어지다 (passive/intransitive suffix) = 끊어지다 (to get cut off). ~거든 is a sentence-final ending that provides background information or justification to the listener — translatable as 'you see,' 'the thing is,' or 'because.' 반말 register (without 요). Hwasa is explaining the broadcast situation to fans.

grammar.meaning: Because, since — connects a reason to a result
If, when — conditional connective ending
There is something to [verb] — expresses existence of a pending task/topic
Passive or intransitive derivation — 'gets/becomes [verbed]'
Sentence-final ending providing background explanation or justification ('you see,' 'the thing is')

sentences.en: So I don't know when it will end
sentences.fr: Donc je ne sais pas quand ça finira

words.notes: Derived from 그렇다 + ~아/어서 (ㅎ-irregular: ㅎ drops). One of the most frequently used conjunctions in Korean, connecting a cause to its result. Sentence-initial position.
Basic question word for time. Here used inside an embedded/indirect question (~(으)ㄹ지 모르다), not as a direct question.
Sino-Korean word (終了) meaning 'end, termination, conclusion.' More formal than 끝. 종료가 되다 = 'to come to an end.' Often used for broadcasts, programs, events.
~(으)ㄹ지 creates an embedded question meaning 'whether' or, combined with a question word like 언제, 'when (it will).' The uncertainty is completed by 모르다.
합쇼체 (formal polite) form of 모르다. Note: 모르다 is a ㅡ-irregular verb (모르 + 아 → 몰라 in 해요체), but conjugates regularly in 합쇼체. Hwasa uses this formal register to address her fan audience politely.

grammar.meaning: To not know whether/when/if — indirect question embedded under 'don't know'
'To become N' or 'for N to happen/be completed'

sentences.en: You know what I'm saying?
sentences.fr: Tu sais ce que je dis ?

words.definition: You know what I mean? / Do you understand?
words.notes: Full English code-switching. K-pop idols commonly mix English into Korean speech. This is a rhetorical discourse marker borrowed from English-speaking hip-hop/R&B culture. Hwasa, as an R&B-influenced artist, uses English phrases naturally. Not uncommon in Korean youth/celebrity speech.

sentences.en: I made a noise like this
sentences.fr: J'ai fait un bruit comme ça

words.notes: 툭 is a sound-symbolic adverb (의태어/의성어) describing a sudden, abrupt action or sound — a pop, tap, or thud. Here unusually nominalized and given the object particle 을. This is a very colloquial, casual usage — treating a sound word as a noun object. The implied full phrase might be 툭 (하는 소리를) 내서.

words.root: 내다 (to produce, to emit, to put out)
words.breakdown: 내 + 서 (= 내 + 어서, vowel contraction)
words.notes: 내다 means 'to produce, emit, put out.' Common in: 소리를 내다 (make a sound), 돈을 내다 (pay money), 결과를 내다 (produce results). ~아/어서 here indicates sequence: 'made (the noise) and then…' The sentence trails off with 이렇게, suggesting a gesture or demonstration followed.

Adverbial form of 이렇다. Part of the three-way demonstrative system: 이렇게 (like this — near speaker), 그렇게 (like that — near listener/known), 저렇게 (like that — distant). Typically accompanied by a physical gesture or demonstration when used in live speech.

grammar.meaning: And then, after doing — sequential connective linking two actions in order
Demonstrative adverb system: 'like this / like that (known) / like that (distant)'

sentences.en: It's a ghost
sentences.fr: C'est un fantôme

words.notes: Sino-Korean word (鬼神). Repeated from sentence 1 — Hwasa is using this as a recurring comedic catchphrase during the broadcast. Repetition for humorous effect is a common speech pattern in Korean variety/live content.
합쇼체 (formal polite) speech level. The overly formal register is part of the joke — a dramatic, announcer-style self-introduction.

grammar.meaning: Copula 'to be' in formal polite declarative form: 'It is N'

sentences.en: I ate too much in Hong Kong
sentences.fr: J'ai trop mangé à Hong Kong

words.notes: Korean transliteration of Hong Kong. Indicates Hwasa has recently been traveling there — likely for a concert, schedule, or personal trip.

words.root: 에서 (at, in — location particle for actions)
words.definition: In, at (where the action takes place)
words.notes: Location particle used for where an action occurs. Compare with 에, which marks static location or destination. 홍콩에서 먹다 = 'eat in Hong Kong' (action at a place).

Originally means 'excessively' (negative nuance), but in modern colloquial Korean also widely used as a positive intensifier ('so, really'). Here retains the original 'too much' meaning, paired with 많이 for emphasis.
Adverbial form of the adjective 많다. 너무 많이 is a very common collocation meaning 'too much' or 'way too much.'

words.definition: Ate (so much) and so… / because I ate
words.notes: ~아/어 가지고 is a colloquial spoken connective equivalent to ~아/어서, expressing cause-and-effect or sequence. Literally involves 가지다 (to hold/carry) but is fully grammaticalized. Very natural in casual speech; often shortened to ~아/어 갖고. The sentence trails off — the consequence (e.g., 배가 불러 'I'm stuffed') is left implied, which is natural in conversational Korean.

grammar.meaning: Colloquial causal/sequential connective — spoken equivalent of ~아/어서 ('because,' 'and then')
At/in — location particle marking where an action takes place

sentences.en: My favorite ghost
sentences.fr: Mon fantôme préféré

words.notes: English code-switching. Most likely Hwasa reading a fan comment from the live chat, responding to her recurring '귀신입니다' joke. K-pop live broadcasts (bstage, VLive, Weverse) feature real-time bilingual fan interaction, so reading English comments aloud is common.

sentences.en: I ate that for the first time today
sentences.fr: J'ai mangé ça pour la première fois aujourd'hui

words.notes: Native Korean word for 'today.' Functions as a time adverb without needing a particle (no 에 required, though 오늘에 is occasionally heard). Part of the set: 어제 (yesterday), 오늘 (today), 내일 (tomorrow).

처음 = 'the first time' or 'the beginning.' ~(으)로 here indicates manner — 'as the first (occasion).' 처음으로 is a set expression. Compare with 처음에 ('at first, in the beginning') which has a different nuance.

Spoken contraction of 그것. Demonstrative pronoun system: 이거 (this, near me), 그거 (that, near you / previously mentioned), 저거 (that, far from both). Here refers to a food item mentioned earlier or being pointed at. No object particle — particle dropping is very common in casual spoken Korean.
반말 (casual) past tense. 먹 + 었 (past tense marker) + 어 (casual ending). No 요 = intimate/casual speech. Hwasa speaks comfortably with fans in 반말 during live broadcasts.

grammar.meaning: Past tense in casual speech level
For the first time — set expression using ~(으)로 for manner
Object particle 을/를 commonly omitted in casual spoken Korean

sentences.en: waffles, eggs
sentences.fr: gaufres, œufs

words.notes: Konglish loanword from English 'waffle.' Widely used in Korean food/café culture. Written in Hangul following Korean phonetic adaptation rules (w → 와, a → ㅏ, ffle → 플).

Konglish loanword from English 'egg.' Korean has native/Sino-Korean words for egg (달걀, 계란), but 에그 is commonly used in food product names and menus: 에그 타르트 (egg tart), 에그 베네딕트 (eggs Benedict), 에그 와플 (egg waffle). Hwasa appears to be listing food items she ate, possibly mid-thought before completing the compound 에그 와플.

sentences.en: Egg waffles?
sentences.fr: Des gaufres aux œufs ?

words.notes: Konglish loanword. Here functioning as a modifier/compound element before 와플.

Konglish loanword. 에그 와플 = 'egg waffle,' a popular Hong Kong street food (鷄蛋仔). The rising intonation (indicated by ?) suggests either Hwasa is confirming the name, asking a fan, or reading a fan comment back as a question.

grammar.meaning: A statement turned into a question purely through rising intonation, without any question particle or ending — very common in casual spoken Korean

sentences.en: It was delicious
sentences.fr: C'était délicieux

words.root: 맛있다 (to be delicious, to be tasty)
words.definition: It was delicious (recalling from personal experience)
words.notes: 맛있다 = 'to be delicious' (맛 'taste' + 있다 'to exist'). ~더라 is a retrospective/recollective sentence-final ending used to report something the speaker personally experienced or witnessed in the past. It conveys 'I recall that…' or 'it turned out that…' 반말 register. This ending is distinctly different from simple past tense ~았/었어 — it emphasizes the speaker's firsthand sensory recall, making it perfect for describing food experiences.

grammar.meaning: Retrospective/recollective ending — reports the speaker's personal past experience or observation: 'I recall that…,' 'it turned out…'

sentences.en: I ate a lot
sentences.fr: j'ai beaucoup mangé

words.definition: A ton, incredibly much, so much
words.notes: Colloquial intensifying adverb meaning 'enormously, incredibly, a huge amount.' Slightly more emphatic and casual than 매우 or 아주. Very common in spoken Korean, especially among younger speakers. Can also appear as 엄청나게 (adverbial form of 엄청나다).

~네 is a sentence-final ending expressing the speaker's mild surprise, realization, or exclamation upon noticing something — 'oh, (I) ate a lot!' or 'wow, I really ate a lot.' 반말 register. Different from ~네요 (해요체 version). Here Hwasa is reflecting on how much she ate with a sense of amused surprise at herself.

grammar.meaning: Exclamatory ending expressing mild surprise, realization, or fresh observation: 'oh!' or 'wow, I see that…'
Past tense combined with exclamatory ending — surprise about a past event or its result

sentences.en: I also ate a lot of egg tarts.
sentences.fr: J'ai aussi mangé beaucoup de tartes aux œufs.

words.notes: Konglish loanword from English 'egg.' Modifies 타르트 to form the compound 에그 타르트.
Konglish loanword from English 'tart.' 에그 타르트 (egg tart) is a famous Hong Kong/Macau pastry (蛋撻), connecting to the earlier mention of eating in Hong Kong.

Additive particle meaning 'also/too.' Replaces the subject or object particle (not stacked on top of them). 에그 타르트도 = 'egg tarts too/also.' This builds a list structure with sentence 19 — 'I ate X too, and Y too.'
Colloquial intensifier. Same usage as in sentence 17.

~고 is the basic conjunctive ending meaning 'and' or 'and then.' Used to connect clauses in sequence or list parallel actions. Here it creates a listing structure: 'I ate egg tarts AND (egg waffles AND…).' The sentence is incomplete on its own — it continues into sentence 19.

grammar.meaning: And, and then — connects clauses by listing parallel actions or events
Also, too — additive particle that replaces 이/가 or 을/를

sentences.en: I also ate a lot of egg waffles.
sentences.fr: J'ai aussi mangé beaucoup de gaufres aux œufs.

words.notes: Konglish loanword. Same as sentence 18.
Konglish loanword. 에그 와플 = egg waffle, the Hong Kong street snack previously mentioned in sentences 14–15.
Additive particle. Parallel structure with sentence 18 — 에그 타르트도 … 먹고, 에그 와플도 … 먹고. This ~도 … ~도 pattern ('X too … Y too') emphasizes that she ate a lot of many different things.
Colloquial intensifier, repeated for emphasis across the listing.

~고 connective ending continuing the list. The trailing ~고 signals the list isn't finished — more items will follow (e.g., 버블티 in sentence 21). This is a natural Korean discourse pattern: stacking multiple V~고 clauses to enumerate actions.

grammar.meaning: And, and then — connects clauses in a list
Both X and Y / X too and Y too — parallel additive structure for emphasis

sentences.en: With that
sentences.fr: Avec ça

words.notes: Spoken contraction of 그것. Refers back to the food items previously listed (에그 타르트, 에그 와플). Part of the demonstrative system: 이거/그거/저거.

Colloquial/spoken equivalent of 과/와 (and/with). Used after a vowel-ending word (그거 ends in ㅓ → 랑). After consonants: 이랑. This particle is characteristic of casual speech — in writing or formal contexts, 과/와 or 하고 would be preferred. The sentence trails off, connecting to sentence 21 (버블티).

grammar.meaning: And, with — colloquial comitative/listing particle (spoken equivalent of 과/와)

sentences.en: bubble tea
sentences.fr: thé à bulles

words.notes: Konglish compound loanword: 버블 from English 'bubble' + 티 from English 'tea.' Refers to the tapioca pearl tea drink originating from Taiwan. Very popular in Korea and Hong Kong. Sometimes also called 밀크티 with 펄 (pearls) or 타피오카 in Korean, but 버블티 is the most common casual term.

sentences.en: So I feel like my stomach will explode
sentences.fr: Alors j'ai l'impression que mon estomac va exploser

words.notes: Derived from 그렇다 + ~아/어서. Connects the previous cause (eating too much) to the result (stomach about to burst). One of the most common Korean conjunctions.
배 is a polysemous word: 'stomach/belly,' 'pear,' 'boat/ship,' or 'multiple (배수).' Context makes it clear this is 'stomach.' 가 marks it as the grammatical subject.
터지다 = 'to burst, explode, pop.' The ~(으)ㄹ prospective modifier form modifies the following bound noun 것. 배가 터지다 is a common hyperbolic expression for being extremely full.

words.root: 것 같다 (to seem like, to feel like)
words.definition: It seems like, I feel like
words.notes: ~(으)ㄹ 것 같다 expresses the speaker's conjecture, feeling, or estimation about something that hasn't happened yet — 'it seems like it will,' 'I feel like it might.' 같아 is 반말 (casual) form of 같다. This is one of the most essential and frequently used Korean grammar patterns at all levels.

grammar.meaning: It seems like (something) will happen / I feel like — conjecture about future or unrealized events
Idiomatic expression: 'stomach bursts' = to be extremely full (hyperbole)

sentences.en: I ate too
sentences.fr: j'ai mangé aussi

words.notes: 밥 literally means 'cooked rice' but in everyday Korean it broadly means 'a meal' or 'food.' 밥 먹다 = 'to eat (a meal)' — one of the most fundamental Korean expressions. Here Hwasa emphasizes that on top of all the snacks, she also ate a proper meal.

Additive particle. Replaces 을 (object particle). 밥도 = 'a meal too / even a meal.' Emphasizes that eating a meal was in addition to all the snacks already listed. Continues the humorous theme of having eaten excessively.
반말 past tense. 먹 + 었 (past) + 어 (casual ending). Consistent with Hwasa's casual speech register throughout the broadcast.

grammar.meaning: Also, too, even — additive particle replacing subject/object markers
Past tense in casual speech level

sentences.en: What flavor bubble tea?
sentences.fr: Quelle saveur de bubble tea ?

words.notes: Interrogative determiner that directly modifies a noun. 무슨 vs. 어떤: 무슨 asks 'what (category/type)?' while 어떤 asks 'what kind of (quality/characteristics)?' 무슨 맛 = 'what flavor?' Hwasa is likely reading and responding to a fan comment about her bubble tea.
Native Korean word for 'taste' or 'flavor.' Used in many compounds: 맛있다 (delicious), 맛없다 (tasteless), 단맛 (sweet taste), 쓴맛 (bitter taste). Here: 무슨 맛 = 'what flavor.'
Konglish compound. Same as sentence 21. The entire sentence is a fragment — a quick question without a verb, which is completely natural in casual spoken Korean.

grammar.meaning: What (kind of) N? — interrogative determiner asking about type or category
In casual speech, the verb/copula can be omitted entirely when context makes the meaning clear

sentences.en: Is it milk tea?
sentences.fr: Est-ce du thé au lait ?

words.notes: Konglish compound loanword: 밀크 from English 'milk' + 티 from English 'tea.' A popular drink variety, especially in Hong Kong-style tea culture (港式奶茶). Hwasa may be guessing the flavor of her bubble tea.

~(이)ㄴ가(요) is an interrogative ending that expresses wondering, uncertainty, or a soft/rhetorical question. Less direct than ~이야? or ~입니까? It carries a musing, self-reflective tone — 'I wonder if it's…' or 'is it maybe…?' Here Hwasa seems to be asking herself or tentatively guessing. 반말 register (no 요).

grammar.meaning: Soft/wondering interrogative — 'is it N?' or 'I wonder if it's N' — expresses uncertainty or musing

sentences.ko: 에그 와플이랑 아이스크림 같이 먹으면 맛있다며
sentences.en: They say it's delicious to eat egg waffles and ice cream together.
sentences.fr: On dit que c'est délicieux de manger des gaufres aux œufs et de la glace ensemble.

words.notes: Konglish compound. The Hong Kong street snack (鷄蛋仔) previously discussed. Takes the particle 이랑 here.
Colloquial comitative/listing particle. 이랑 after consonant (와플 ends in ㄹ), 랑 after vowel. Spoken equivalent of 과/와. 에그 와플이랑 아이스크림 = 'egg waffle and ice cream.'
Konglish loanword from English 'ice cream.' Fully naturalized in Korean. Sometimes abbreviated to 아이스 in casual speech (though 아이스 can also mean 'iced' as in 아이스 아메리카노).
Adverb meaning 'together.' Can also function as a particle meaning 'like' (N같이 = like N), but here it is clearly the adverb 'together.' 같이 먹다 = 'to eat together (combined).'
~(으)면 conditional ending. 먹 ends in ㄱ (consonant) so 으 is inserted: 먹으면. 'If you eat (egg waffles and ice cream together)…'

words.definition: They say it's delicious / (I heard) it's delicious, right?
words.notes: ~다며 is a contracted form of ~다면서 (= ~다고 하면서), which combines indirect quotation (~다고) with ~(으)면서 ('while' or 'and'). As a sentence-final ending, ~다며(요) means 'I heard that…, is that right?' or 'people say that…, right?' It conveys hearsay while seeking confirmation. 반말 register. Hwasa is relaying something she heard (or a fan comment) and checking if it's true.

grammar.meaning: If, when — conditional connective
Reported hearsay + confirmation seeking: 'I heard that… (is it true?)' or 'they say that…, right?'
And, with — colloquial comitative particle

sentences.en: I ate Porobao
sentences.fr: J'ai mangé du Porobao

words.definition: Porobao — a Hong Kong-style pineapple bun (菠蘿包)
words.notes: Korean transliteration of the Cantonese 菠蘿包 (bo lo baau), meaning 'pineapple bun.' A signature Hong Kong bakery item with a sweet, crumbly topping resembling a pineapple's surface (it doesn't actually contain pineapple). The Korean spelling 뽀로바오 uses the tense consonant ㅃ to approximate the Cantonese initial. A must-try Hong Kong street food.
반말 past tense. Note the object particle (을) is dropped — 뽀로바오(를) 먹었어. Particle dropping is standard in casual speech.

grammar.meaning: Past tense in casual speech level
을/를 commonly omitted in casual spoken Korean

sentences.ko: 한 아주 사랑스러운 팬 친구가 뽀로바오를
sentences.en: A very lovely fan friend bought Porobao.
sentences.fr: Un très charmant ami fan a acheté Porobao.

words.notes: 한 before a noun functions similarly to the English indefinite article 'a/an.' Derived from 하나 (one). 한 + noun = 'a certain (noun)' or 'one (noun).' Here: 한 팬 친구 = 'a (certain) fan friend.'
Intensifying adverb. Slightly more neutral/standard than the colloquial 엄청. Modifies the following adjective 사랑스러운.
사랑 (love) + ~스럽다 (suffix creating adjectives meaning 'having the quality of'). 사랑스럽다 = 'to be loveable/adorable.' The ~(으)ㄴ adnominal form (사랑스러운) modifies the noun 팬 친구. ㅂ-irregular: 스럽 + 은 → 스러운.
Konglish loanword from English 'fan.' Standard term in K-pop culture. 팬 친구 = 'fan friend' — an affectionate way idols refer to their fans, positioning them as friends rather than just followers.

친구 = 'friend.' 가 is the subject particle (after vowel). 팬 친구가 = 'a fan friend (subject).' The sentence appears to trail off — the verb (presumably 사줬어 'bought for me' or similar) is implied or continues in the next utterance.

Same food item as sentence 27. Here the object particle 를 is explicitly used (contrast with sentence 27 where it was dropped). The sentence is incomplete — it trails off, a common feature of natural spoken Korean where the speaker changes direction mid-thought.

grammar.meaning: 'A (certain)' — functions like an indefinite article before a noun
Suffix creating adjectives meaning 'having the quality of N' (N + 스럽다)
Adjective stems ending in ㅂ change to 우 before vowel endings (스럽 → 스러운)
Trailing off mid-sentence — very common in natural spoken Korean, where context or the next utterance completes the thought

sentences.en: As soon as I arrived in Hong Kong, it was really like this.
sentences.fr: Dès mon arrivée à Hong Kong, c'était vraiment comme ça.

words.notes: Korean transliteration. No particle attached — in casual speech, the destination/location particle (에) is often dropped. Full form would be 홍콩에 도착하자마자.

도착 (Sino-Korean 到着 = arrival) + 하다 (to do). ~자마자 is a connective ending meaning 'as soon as' — the second action happens immediately after the first. No tense marker is added to the first clause with ~자마자. This is a very useful and commonly tested grammar point.

words.root: 진짜 (really, for real / the real thing)
words.notes: 진짜 as a noun means 'the real thing' (vs. 가짜 'fake'). As an adverb (the usage here), it means 'really, truly, seriously.' Extremely common in colloquial Korean as an intensifier. Similar to 정말 but more casual.

Demonstrative adverb 'like this.' Here the sentence trails off — Hwasa is likely gesturing or demonstrating something (perhaps mimicking receiving food, or showing how much she ate). The incomplete sentence combined with 이렇게 strongly implies a physical demonstration that the audio transcript cannot capture.

grammar.meaning: As soon as — the second event happens immediately after the first
Location/destination particle 에 omitted in casual speech

sentences.en: like this
sentences.fr: comme ça

words.notes: Demonstrative adverb from the 이- (proximal) series. Standalone utterance — Hwasa is continuing from sentence 29, almost certainly accompanied by a gesture or physical demonstration. In live broadcasts, 이렇게 on its own is a verbal cue that the speaker is showing something visually.

sentences.en: I gave them a few boxes.
sentences.fr: Je leur ai donné quelques cartons.

words.notes: 몇 can be interrogative ('how many?') or indefinite ('a few, several'). Here it is indefinite: 'a few (boxes).' When interrogative, it appears in questions (몇 개? = how many?). When indefinite like here, it indicates an unspecified small number.
상자 (箱子) = box, carton. Sino-Korean word. 를 is the object particle after a vowel-ending noun. Refers to boxes of 뽀로바오 (pineapple buns) that the fan brought.

반말 past tense of 주다. 주 + 었어 contracts to 줬어 in speech and informal writing. 주다 = 'to give.' The indirect object (to whom) is implied from context — likely the staff/team. Note: the English/French translations say 'I gave them' but the Korean subject could also be the fan who gave Hwasa the boxes. Context from sentence 28 suggests the fan gave them.

grammar.meaning: A few, several — indefinite small quantity
Past tense in casual speech

sentences.ko: 그래서 스탭이랑 다 같이 나눠 먹었어
sentences.en: So I shared it with the staff.
sentences.fr: Je l'ai donc partagé avec le staff.

words.notes: Causal conjunction connecting the previous context (received boxes of food) to the result (shared with staff).

Konglish loanword from English 'staff.' In Korean entertainment, 스탭 (also written 스태프) refers to the production/management crew, stylists, managers, etc. who work with the artist. Very commonly used in K-pop/entertainment contexts.
Colloquial comitative particle after consonant-ending noun (스탭 ends in ㅂ). 스탭이랑 = 'with the staff.' Spoken equivalent of 스탭과.
Adverb meaning 'all, entirely, everyone.' 다 같이 = 'all together.' Here it emphasizes that everyone on the team shared the food.
Adverb meaning 'together.' 다 같이 is a very common set phrase meaning 'all together.'
나누다 = 'to divide, to share, to split.' 나누 + 어 contracts to 나눠. Part of the compound verb 나눠 먹다.

words.root: 나눠 먹다 (to share food, to split and eat)
words.notes: 나눠 먹다 is a compound verb meaning 'to share (food) and eat it together.' Very common expression in Korean food culture, reflecting the communal eating tradition. 나눠 is the ~아/어 connective form of 나누다 linking to 먹다. Past tense 반말.

grammar.meaning: Two verbs combined where V1 describes the manner of V2
Together with N — comitative construction

sentences.en: There's one left here
sentences.fr: Il en reste un ici

words.notes: Proximal place pronoun. Part of the set: 여기 (here), 거기 (there, near listener), 저기 (over there). No particle needed — 여기 can function as a location adverb on its own in casual speech (여기에 would be more complete).

Native Korean number 'one.' Used here without a counter (개 would be typical: 하나 = one piece/item). Dropping the counter is natural in casual speech when the item is contextually clear (one pineapple bun remaining).

words.definition: There is (one) remaining, but… / there's one left and…
words.notes: 남다 (to remain) + ~아 있다 (resultative state = the state of having remained) = 남아있다 (to be left over, to remain). ~는 is the present tense adnominal ending, but here it's part of ~는데. ~(으)ㄴ/는데 is a versatile connective ending that provides background information, sets up contrast, or softly leads into the next statement. Here: 'there's one left (and…)' — trailing off, inviting the listener to see it or react.

grammar.meaning: Resultative state — the ongoing result of a completed action ('is in the state of having V-ed')
Background/context-setting connective ending — 'but,' 'and (so),' or providing a soft lead-in

sentences.en: The food here was delicious
sentences.fr: La nourriture ici était délicieuse

words.notes: Proximal place pronoun. Refers to Hong Kong or a specific restaurant/area in Hong Kong.

Spoken contraction of 것. 여기 거 = 여기 것 = 'the stuff/things from here' or 'the ones here.' In food contexts, this is a casual way of saying 'the food here' or 'what they have here.' The possessive/origin pattern N + 거/것 is extremely common: 나 거 (mine), 여기 거 (the one from here), 그 집 거 (that place's stuff).

Same pattern as sentence 16. ~더라 is a retrospective sentence-final ending conveying firsthand past experience: 'I recall it was delicious.' 반말 register. The speaker is sharing a personal sensory memory — perfect for food commentary.

grammar.meaning: Retrospective ending — reports the speaker's personal past experience: 'I recall that…'
'The one(s) of/from N' — casual possessive or origin marker

sentences.en: There's one left, one
sentences.fr: Il en reste un, un

words.notes: Native Korean number 'one.' Appears twice in this sentence — at the beginning and repeated at the end for emphasis. This repetition is a natural spoken Korean pattern for emphasis or playful stress: 'one left — just one!'

words.root: 남다 (to remain, to be left over)
words.notes: 반말 past tense of 남다. While technically past tense, 남았어 describes the current resulting state: 'there is one remaining (as a result of the others being eaten).' Compare with 남아있어 (sentence 33) which uses the explicit resultative ~아 있다 pattern — 남았어 achieves a similar meaning more concisely.

grammar.meaning: Repeating a word at the end of the sentence for emphasis — natural in casual spoken Korean

sentences.en: I also ate a lot of egg tarts
sentences.fr: J'ai aussi mangé beaucoup de tartelettes aux œufs

words.notes: Konglish compound: 에그 (egg) + 타르트 (tart). The famous Hong Kong/Macau pastry (蛋撻). Previously mentioned in sentence 18.
Additive particle replacing the object particle 를. 에그 타르트도 = 'egg tarts too/also.' Continues the theme of listing all the things she ate excessively.
Colloquial intensifier. Recurring throughout this broadcast segment, reinforcing the humorous 'I ate way too much' narrative.

반말 past tense. Note this sentence is a complete version of what was said more fragmentarily in sentence 18 (에그 타르트도 엄청 먹고) — there the trailing ~고 connected to the next clause, while here ~었어 closes the statement.

grammar.meaning: Also, too — additive particle

sentences.ko: 에그 타르트도 베이크 하우스 거 엄청 먹었고
sentences.en: I also ate a lot of egg tarts from Bake House.
sentences.fr: J'ai aussi mangé beaucoup de tartelettes aux œufs de Bake House.

words.notes: Konglish compound. Same item — now Hwasa specifies which egg tarts she ate.
Additive particle. Repeated pattern from the listing structure.

Konglish proper noun — the name of a specific bakery, likely a well-known Hong Kong establishment famous for egg tarts. Could refer to 'Tai Cheong Bakery' or another popular spot. The name uses English words transliterated into Korean.

words.definition: The ones from (Bake House), their stuff
words.notes: Contracted form of 것. 베이크 하우스 거 = 'Bake House's (ones)' or 'the ones from Bake House.' Same possessive/origin pattern as 여기 거 (sentence 34). Functions like a casual possessive: [place name] + 거 = 'the stuff/products from [place].'
Colloquial intensifier. Consistent usage throughout.

Past tense ~었 combined with the listing connective ~고. 먹었고 = 'ate (this) and (also)…' The ~고 signals the list continues — she's about to mention another place or item. Note: ~았/었고 (past + and) vs. ~고 alone (present/general + and).

grammar.meaning: 'The ones from N' or 'N's stuff' — casual possessive construction
Past tense + listing connective: 'did X and (also)…'

sentences.en: It's a really good restaurant there, right?
sentences.fr: C'est un très bon restaurant là-bas, non ?

words.notes: Medial place pronoun — 'there' (a place the listener knows about or that was just mentioned). Part of the set: 여기/거기/저기. Refers to Bake House.
Colloquial intensifier. Modifies the implicit copula or assessment: '(it's) really (a) 맛집.'

words.definition: A great restaurant, a famous food spot
words.notes: Popular compound word: 맛 (taste/flavor) + 집 (house/establishment). 맛집 specifically means a restaurant known for its delicious food — a 'must-eat' spot. Widely used in Korean food culture, review apps (like 맛집 리스트), and social media. Not just any restaurant, but one with a reputation for great food.

Contracted form of 그렇지 (그렇다 + ~지). ~지 is a sentence-final ending seeking agreement or confirmation ('right?'). 그렇지 → 그지 is a very casual spoken contraction. 반말 register. Hwasa is asking fans to confirm that the restaurant is indeed good. Similar in function to English tag questions.

grammar.meaning: Right? Isn't it? — seeks agreement or confirmation from the listener
Contracted spoken form of 그렇지 ('isn't that so? / right?')

sentences.ko: 역시 현지 팬이 추천해주는 건 다르다니까
sentences.en: After all, what local fans recommend is different.
sentences.fr: Après tout, ce que recommandent les fans locaux est différent.

words.definition: As expected, after all, sure enough
words.notes: Sino-Korean origin (亦是). Expresses that something turned out as one might expect or confirms a known truth. Nuance: 'just as you'd think,' 'sure enough,' 'as expected.' Here: 'as expected, local fan recommendations are on another level.'

Sino-Korean word (現地) meaning 'the local area' or 'on location.' 현지 팬 = 'local fans' (i.e., Hong Kong-based fans, as opposed to international or Korean fans). Commonly used: 현지인 (local person), 현지 음식 (local food), 현지 시간 (local time).
Konglish loanword + subject particle 이 (after consonant). The local fans are the subject who perform the recommending.

추천하다 (推薦, to recommend) + ~아/어 주다 (to do something as a favor/benefit for someone). 추천해주다 = 'to recommend (for someone else's benefit).' The ~아/어 주다 auxiliary adds the nuance that the action benefits the receiver — the fans recommended places for Hwasa's benefit. ~는 is the present tense adnominal ending, modifying 건.

words.definition: The thing that… / what (they recommend) — as topic
words.notes: Contracted form of 것은. 추천해주는 건 = 'what (they) recommend (topic).' Creates a nominalized clause acting as the topic of the sentence: 'the thing that local fans recommend (topic) is different.'

다르다 = 'to be different, to be distinct.' ~다니까(요) is a sentence-final ending expressing emphatic assertion or mild frustration that the listener should already know or accept this: 'I'm telling you (it's different)!' or 'I keep saying (it's different)!' Combines indirect quotation ~다고 + ~(으)니까 (because/since). 반말 register. Hwasa is enthusiastically insisting on the superiority of local fan recommendations.

grammar.meaning: To do something for someone's benefit — benefactive auxiliary verb
Turns a verb clause into a noun phrase: 'the thing/act of V-ing' or 'what someone V-s'
Emphatic assertion ending: 'I'm telling you that…!' — expresses insistence or mild exasperation

sentences.en: But here it is done the same way
sentences.fr: Mais ici, c'est pareil

words.notes: Contracted spoken form of 그런데. Extremely common in casual speech. Functions as a topic-shifter or mild contrast marker. One of the most frequently used connectors in spoken Korean.
여기 = 'here.' In this context, Hwasa is referring to the Hong Kong FWD Champions Day event at Sha Tin Racecourse where she just performed. 가 is the subject particle (after vowel).

words.definition: in exactly the same way; identically
words.notes: Adverbial form of 똑같다. 똑 is an intensifying prefix meaning 'exactly/precisely,' and 같다 means 'to be the same.' The ~이 ending converts the adjective to an adverb. Hwasa is saying the fans here (in Hong Kong) did the same thing as fans elsewhere — wearing the crown headbands.

Adverbial form of the demonstrative adjective 이렇다 ('to be like this'). ~게 converts adjectives to adverbs. Part of the 이/그/저 demonstrative series: 이렇게 (like this, near speaker), 그렇게 (like that, near listener), 저렇게 (like that, far from both). Hwasa is likely gesturing while speaking.

words.definition: did (it) like that, and so…; having done (it)…
words.notes: 해가지고 is a very common colloquial connective form, equivalent to 해서 ('having done, and so…'). It comes from 하다 + 아/어 가지고. The pattern V-아/어 가지고 is the spoken/casual equivalent of V-아/어서, expressing cause-result or sequential action. Often further contracted to 해갖고 in very casual speech. This is characteristic of natural spoken Korean and appears frequently in interviews and vlogs. The sentence trails off, implying the result is obvious or will be stated next.

grammar.meaning: Contracted form of the conjunction 'but/however/by the way' — standard in spoken Korean
Colloquial connective equivalent to V-아/어서: 'having done V, and so…' — very common in spoken Korean
Converts a descriptive verb/adjective to an adverb

sentences.en: It was so cute
sentences.fr: C'était si mignon

words.notes: Positive intensifier, as in previous sentences. Colloquial usage where 너무 simply means 'very/so' without negative connotation.

귀엽다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective. When the stem ending ㅂ meets a vowel suffix, ㅂ changes to 우: 귀엽 → 귀여우 + 었 → 귀여웠. The final 어 is the casual 반말/해체 ending. ㅂ-irregular conjugation is a key grammar point for beginners. Hwasa is describing how cute the fans looked wearing their crown headbands at the Hong Kong event.

grammar.meaning: When a stem ending in ㅂ meets a vowel suffix, ㅂ changes to 우 (e.g., 귀엽 + 어 → 귀여워)
Past tense + casual 반말/해체 ending for descriptive verbs

sentences.en: So my gas raiding was successful.
sentences.fr: Mon raid au gaz a donc réussi.

words.notes: Derived from 그렇다 ('to be so') + ~(으)니까 ('because/since'). Used to draw a conclusion or restate a point. Can mean 'so therefore' (conclusion) or 'I mean / what I'm saying is' (clarification). Here it introduces Hwasa's humorous conclusion.

나 = casual first-person pronoun. 의 = possessive particle ('of'). 나의 is the full form; in casual speech it often contracts to 내. Here Hwasa uses the full form 나의 for slightly more emphatic/playful effect.

This is a playful Konglish coinage by Hwasa. It is a humorous distortion of 가스라이팅 (gaslighting), the Korean buzzword borrowed from English 'gaslighting' (manipulating someone into questioning their reality). 가스라이팅 became a major Korean buzzword around 2021-2022 and was even selected as a top new word of the year. Hwasa jokingly says she 'gaslighted' her fans into wearing crown headbands to the event — she convinced/persuaded them so effectively that they all showed up wearing them. The ~레이딩 (raiding) variant may be intentional wordplay mixing 'gaslighting' with 'raiding' (a fan event term), or simply her playful mispronunciation. 이 is the subject particle (after consonant).

성공 (成功) = 'success' (Sino-Korean). 하다 = 'to do.' ~(으)ㄴ is the past/completed modifier ending, turning the verb into a relative clause modifying 거 (것). 성공한 거 = 'a thing that succeeded' = 'it was a success.'

거 is the contracted spoken form of 것. ~지 is a sentence-final ending expressing confirmation or seeking agreement — 'right?' / 'isn't it?' / 'you see.' In 반말 register. The pattern ~(으)ㄴ/는 거지 = 'it's that…, you see' / 'so it means that…, right?' Hwasa is playfully confirming her own conclusion. Note: 거지 as a single unit here should not be confused with the homophone 거지 meaning 'beggar.'

grammar.meaning: Explanatory/confirmatory pattern: 'so it's that…, right?' / 'that means…, you see' (반말)
Past/completed modifier forming a relative clause
Sentence-final ending seeking or asserting confirmation: 'right?' / 'you know'

sentences.en: So it was so funny
sentences.fr: Alors c'était tellement drôle

words.definition: so; I mean; like I said
words.notes: Same usage as sentence 62. Here it reinforces and re-emphasizes the point — 'I'm telling you, it was so funny.'
Intensifier, same colloquial positive usage as throughout this transcript.

words.root: 웃기다 (to be funny; to make someone laugh)
words.definition: it was funny, I'm telling you
words.notes: 웃기다 is the causative form of 웃다 ('to laugh'): 'to make (someone) laugh' → 'to be funny.' Past tense: 웃겼다 (웃기 + 었 + 다). The ending ~다고 is the indirect quotation particle (from ~다고 하다, 'to say that…'), but here used without the 하다 verb as an emphatic sentence-final form. This is a very common colloquial pattern: ending a sentence with ~다고 to emphasize or insist on what one is saying — 'I'm telling you it was funny!' / 'it was SO funny, I say!' This truncated quotation form is characteristic of animated, emotional spoken Korean.

grammar.meaning: Indirect quotation ending used sentence-finally without 하다 to emphasize or insist: 'I'm telling you that…!'
Causative derivation: 웃다 ('to laugh') → 웃기다 ('to make laugh / to be funny')

sentences.en: You can't throw it away
sentences.fr: Tu ne peux pas le jeter

words.notes: 버리다 = 'to throw away/discard.' ~(으)면 is the conditional ending: 'if.' 버리면 = 'if you throw it away.' Note: 버리다 as a main verb means 'to discard,' but it is also very commonly used as an auxiliary verb (V-아/어 버리다) meaning 'to completely finish V-ing' with a nuance of finality or relief. Here it is the main verb.

words.definition: it's not allowed; you must not; you can't
words.notes: 안 되다 = 'to not be okay / to not be allowed.' The conjugation 되 + 어 contracts to 돼 (a common point of confusion for learners — 돼 vs 되). 버리면 안 돼 is the standard prohibition pattern: V-(으)면 안 되다 = 'you must not V / it's not okay to V.' 반말 register. Hwasa is playfully telling fans not to throw away their crown headbands. The polite form would be 버리면 안 돼요.

grammar.meaning: Prohibition pattern: 'you must not V / it's not allowed to V / you can't V'
Conditional ending: 'if'

sentences.en: It was lovely, really so cute
sentences.fr: C'était charmant, vraiment trop mignon

words.definition: it was lovely; they were adorable
words.notes: 사랑 ('love') + 스럽다 (suffix meaning 'having the quality of'). 사랑스럽다 = 'to be lovable/adorable.' This is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: 스럽 + 었 → 스러웠 (ㅂ → 우 before vowel). The ~스럽다 suffix is productive and appears in many adjectives: 자연스럽다 ('natural'), 걱정스럽다 ('worrisome'), etc. 반말 past tense ending 어.
Colloquial intensifier, same usage as in previous sentences. Here it modifies the following phrase 'so cute야.'

This is a code-switching moment where Hwasa uses the English phrase 'so cute' and attaches the Korean 반말 copula ending ~야 (from 이다). This is very common in modern Korean pop culture — mixing English words/phrases with Korean grammar endings. Notably, 'So Cute' is also the title of one of Hwasa's songs, which she performed at this very event (the FWD Champions Day at Sha Tin Racecourse, Hong Kong on April 26, 2026). So this may be a deliberate self-reference as well as a natural expression.

grammar.meaning: Adjectives ending in ~스럽다 follow ㅂ-irregular conjugation: ㅂ → 우 before vowel suffixes
Attaching the Korean copula 이다 to an English word/phrase — common in colloquial modern Korean
Suffix meaning 'having the quality/feeling of N' — forms descriptive adjectives from nouns

sentences.ko: 근데 진짜 홍콩에 원관을 쓴 멍청이들이 진짜 많았어
sentences.en: But there really were a lot of idiots in Hong Kong who wore official crowns.
sentences.fr: Mais il y avait vraiment beaucoup d'idiots à Hong Kong qui portaient des couronnes officielles.

words.notes: Contracted spoken form of 그런데, same as sentence 60.
Used twice in this sentence for double emphasis — a hallmark of excited, emphatic spoken Korean. First 진짜 modifies the whole statement, second 진짜 directly modifies 많았어.

홍콩 is the Korean rendering of 'Hong Kong' (from Cantonese). 에 is the static location particle ('in/at'). Hwasa is referring to her performance at the FWD Champions Day event at Sha Tin Racecourse in Hong Kong on April 26, 2026, where she performed 'So Cute,' 'Twit,' and 'Good Goodbye.'
Same fandom term as in previous sentences. News reports from the event confirm that fans at Sha Tin waited 'with support boards and crown headbands.' 을 is the object particle.
Past/completed modifier ~(으)ㄴ forming a relative clause: '멍청이들 who wore 원관.' Same usage as sentence 55.
Same affectionate fandom name. 이 is the subject particle (after consonant).

words.definition: there were many; there were a lot
words.notes: 많다 = 'to be many/much.' Regular conjugation: 많 + 았 + 어. 반말 past tense. 진짜 많았어 = 'there really were a lot (of them).'

grammar.meaning: Past modifier forming a relative clause: 'Noun who/that V-ed'
Location particle indicating where something exists or an event takes place
Repeating an adverb in a single sentence to intensify emphasis — characteristic of spoken Korean

sentences.en: I won't lie
sentences.fr: je ne mentirai pas

words.notes: 거짓 = 'false/fake' + 말 = 'words/speech.' Together: 'false words' = 'a lie.' Native Korean compound noun.
Short-form negation, placed before the verb 치다.

words.root: 치다 (to hit; to play; to tell [a lie])
words.definition: telling (a lie) — here negated: 'not telling a lie'
words.notes: 치다 has many meanings ('to hit,' 'to strike,' 'to play piano,' etc.). In the collocation 거짓말(을) 치다, it means 'to tell a lie.' This is a more colloquial/emphatic variant of 거짓말(을) 하다. The ~고 connective links this to the following statement: 'not lying, (I tell you that)…' The whole phrase 거짓말 안 치고 is a set expression functioning as a discourse marker meaning 'no lie' / 'honestly' / 'I'm not kidding.' The object particle 을 is dropped, which is common in casual speech.

grammar.meaning: Negation pattern placing 안 before the verb
Colloquial collocation: 'to tell a lie' (more emphatic/casual than 거짓말하다)
Connective ~고 used to frame the following statement: 'doing X, (I say that)…'

sentences.en: It was really powerful
sentences.fr: C'était vraiment puissant

words.notes: Colloquial intensifier, consistent usage throughout this transcript.

words.root: 힘(이) 되다 (to be a source of strength/support)
words.definition: it gave me strength; it was empowering; it was a source of energy
words.notes: 힘(이) 되다 literally means 'to become strength' → 'to be a source of strength/encouragement/support.' This is a common and warm expression: 힘이 됐어 = 'it gave me strength / it was so encouraging.' The subject particle 이 is dropped in casual speech, and 되 + 었 contracts to 됐 (되 + 었 → 됐). Hwasa is saying that seeing all the fans in crown headbands was truly empowering for her. Compare with 힘(이) 나다 (sentence 54, 'to feel energized') — similar meaning but 되다 implies the fans WERE the source of strength, while 나다 focuses on the energy arising within oneself. Also compare with 힘들다 (sentence 56, 'to be hard/tough') which looks similar but has opposite emotional valence.

grammar.meaning: Idiomatic expression: 'to be a source of strength/encouragement/support'
The verb 되다 in past tense contracts: 되 + 었 → 됐. This is standard orthography, not just a spoken shortcut.

sentences.ko: 그러니까 색깔도 분홍색이랑 보라색 섞어가지고 어딜 가도 다 눈에 띄어
sentences.en: So, the colors are a mixture of pink and purple, so it stands out wherever you go.
sentences.fr: Ainsi, les couleurs sont un mélange de rose et de violet, ce qui fait qu'il se démarque partout où vous allez.

words.definition: so; I mean; the thing is
words.notes: Same conjunction as sentences 62 and 63. Here it introduces an explanation of WHY the crown headbands stood out so much — because of their colors.

words.definition: the colors too; even the colors
words.notes: 색깔 is a native Korean word for 'color' (slightly more colloquial/spoken than the Sino-Korean 색 alone, though 색 also appears in compound color words below). 도 = 'also/too/even,' here implying 'on top of everything else, the colors ALSO (contributed to standing out).' The particle adds cumulative emphasis.

분홍색 (粉紅色) = 'pink' (literally 'powder-red color'). Sino-Korean. 이랑 is the casual/spoken listing particle meaning 'and/with' (used after consonant). It is the colloquial equivalent of 과/와. The formal written equivalents are 과 (after consonant) and 와 (after vowel). ~(이)랑 is characteristic of spoken Korean and 반말 register.
보라 = 'purple/violet' (native Korean) + 색 (色, 'color,' Sino-Korean). A hybrid compound. 보라색 is the standard word for purple in Korean.

words.definition: mixed (them) together, and so…; having mixed…
words.notes: 섞다 = 'to mix/blend.' The pattern V-아/어 가지고 is the colloquial equivalent of V-아/어서 ('having done V, and so…'), as seen in sentence 60 (해가지고). 섞어가지고 = 'having mixed / because they're mixed.' This connects the cause (the colors are mixed pink and purple) to the result (they stand out). Very natural spoken Korean — in writing this would more likely be 섞어서.

어디 = 'where.' 를 is the object/direction particle, contracted: 어디를 → 어딜. This contraction is standard in spoken Korean. 어딜 가도 = 'no matter where you go / wherever you go.' The object particle 를 with movement verbs indicates direction.

words.definition: even if (you) go; no matter where (you) go
words.notes: V-아/어도 is the concessive connective meaning 'even if V / no matter if V.' 가 + 도 → 가도 = 'even if (one) goes.' Combined with 어딜: 어딜 가도 = 'no matter where you go / wherever you go.' This is a very common and useful pattern.
Emphasizes totality — 'they ALL stand out' / 'everywhere without exception they catch your eye.'

words.root: 눈에 띄다 (to stand out, to catch one's eye)
words.definition: stands out; catches your eye; is noticeable
words.notes: 눈 = 'eye.' 에 = location particle. 띄다 = 'to be caught/noticed' (related to 뜨다, 'to float/rise'). 눈에 띄다 is a set idiomatic expression meaning 'to stand out / to catch the eye / to be conspicuous.' The conjugation 띄 + 어 → 띄어 (반말 sentence ending). Hwasa is explaining that the pink-and-purple mixed colors of the crown headbands made them extremely visible and eye-catching wherever she looked in the crowd. This is a very useful intermediate-level idiom.

grammar.meaning: Colloquial connective equivalent to V-아/어서: 'having done V, and so…' — characteristic of spoken Korean
Concessive pattern with interrogative: 'no matter where one V-s / wherever one V-s'
Concessive connective: 'even if V / no matter if V'
Casual/spoken listing particle: 'and / with' — colloquial equivalent of 과/와
Idiomatic expression: 'to stand out / to catch one's eye / to be conspicuous'
Spoken contraction of the interrogative pronoun + object particle: 어디를 → 어딜

sentences.ko: 근데 모든 멍청이들이 아랑곳하지 않고 그 원관을 쓰고 앉아있었는데 얼마나 귀여웠는지 몰라
sentences.en: But all the idiots didn't care and just sat there wearing that crown. You can't tell how cute it was.
sentences.fr: Mais tous les idiots s'en fichaient et restaient assis là, portant cette couronne. Vous ne pouvez pas dire à quel point c'était mignon.

words.notes: Contracted spoken form of 그런데. Standard casual speech connector, consistent throughout this transcript.
A determiner (관형사) that always precedes a noun. 모든 멍청이들 = 'all the Twits / every single Twit.' Unlike 다 (adverb), 모든 functions as a noun modifier. Cannot stand alone — must modify a following noun.
Same affectionate fandom name. 이 is the subject particle (after consonant).

words.definition: without caring; not minding at all
words.notes: 아랑곳하다 is a somewhat literary/elevated verb meaning 'to care about / to pay heed to.' It is almost exclusively used in the negative: 아랑곳하지 않다 = 'to not care at all / to pay no mind.' 아랑곳 is a bound noun of uncertain etymology that only appears in this collocation. The pattern V-지 않다 is the long-form negation ('does not V'). ~고 connects to the next action: 'didn't care AND (just sat there).' This is a more sophisticated vocabulary choice — Hwasa is emphasizing that the fans were completely unfazed and proudly wore their crowns regardless of anything.
Demonstrative determiner from the 이/그/저 series. 그 = 'that' (something already mentioned or known to both speaker and listener). 그 원관 = 'that crown (headband we've been talking about).'
Same fandom-specific crown/wreath accessory discussed throughout. 을 is the object particle.

쓰다 = 'to wear on the head.' ~고 here connects the manner/state to the main posture verb 앉아있다: 'wearing the crown AND sitting.' This creates an image of simultaneous actions — they sat there while wearing the crowns.

words.root: 앉아있다 (to be sitting, to be seated)
words.notes: 앉다 = 'to sit.' 앉아있다 = 앉다 + 아/어 있다, which is the resultative state pattern: 'to be in the state of having sat down' = 'to be sitting/seated.' This is different from 앉고 있다 (the act of sitting down in progress). Past tense 었 + the connective ~는데 (background/setup). The whole phrase paints a vivid picture: the fans were just sitting there calmly, crowned, completely unbothered — and sets up the emotional payoff that follows.
Interrogative adverb used in the exclamatory/rhetorical pattern 얼마나 ~ (으)ㄴ/는지 모르다. Here it does not ask a real question but expresses intensity: 'you have no idea HOW cute it was.'

귀엽다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: 귀엽 → 귀여우 + 었 → 귀여웠. The ending ~(으)ㄴ/는지 creates an indirect question or embedded clause: 'whether/how…' When combined with 모르다, it forms the exclamatory idiom: 'you don't know how cute it was' = 'it was unbelievably cute.'

words.definition: you don't know; you can't imagine
words.notes: 모르다 = 'to not know.' Irregular conjugation: 모르 + 아 → 몰라 (르-irregular: ㄹ doubles and ㅡ drops). In the pattern 얼마나 ~(으)ㄴ/는지 몰라, it is rhetorical/exclamatory: 'you have no idea (how cute it was)!' 반말 sentence ending. This is one of the most expressive and commonly used exclamatory patterns in Korean.

grammar.meaning: Long-form negation: 'to not V'
Expresses the ongoing state resulting from a completed action: 'to be in the state of having V-ed'
Exclamatory/rhetorical pattern: 'you have no idea how ~ / it was incredibly ~'
Sets up background context or situation before the main emotional reaction
When a stem ending in 르 meets 아/어, ㄹ doubles and ㅡ drops: 모르 + 아 → 몰라

sentences.en: Real cuteness conquers everything
sentences.fr: La vraie gentillesse triomphe de tout

words.notes: Here 진짜 functions as a noun modifier ('real/genuine') rather than an adverb ('really'). 진짜 귀여움 = 'real/true cuteness.' It modifies the noun 귀여움 directly.

귀엽다 → 귀여움 via the nominalizing suffix ~(으)ㅁ, which turns a verb/adjective into a noun. ㅂ-irregular: 귀엽 → 귀여우 + ㅁ → 귀여움. This is distinct from the ~기 nominalizer — ~(으)ㅁ tends to create more abstract/permanent noun concepts. 은 is the topic marker, setting up 귀여움 as the sentence topic: 'as for (true) cuteness…' Compare: 귀여움 = 'cuteness' (state/concept), 귀엽기 = 'being cute' (action/process).
Same determiner as in sentence 70. Modifies the bound noun 것 (contracted to 걸).
걸 is the contracted spoken form of 것을. 모든 걸 = 모든 것을 = 'everything (as an object).' This contraction is extremely common in spoken Korean. 것 → 거 (casual) and 것을 → 걸 (casual + particle).

words.root: 이기다 (to win, to conquer, to overcome)
words.notes: 이기다 = 'to win/defeat/overcome.' Conjugation: 이기 + 어 → 이겨 (기 + 어 contracts to 겨). 반말 sentence ending. This sentence is a playful declaration by Hwasa — 'true cuteness conquers all!' — referring to how adorable her fans looked in their crown headbands. It has the feel of a catchphrase or maxim.

grammar.meaning: Suffix that turns a verb/adjective into an abstract noun: V → 'the act/state of V'
Spoken contraction of the bound noun 것 + object particle 을
Topic marker used to make a general/universal statement about the topic

sentences.ko: 스탭 언니들도 팬들 다 원관 쓰고 있더라 이러면서 너무 귀여워하는 거야
sentences.en: The staff and fans are all wearing circle crowns and they think it's so cute.
sentences.fr: Le staff et les fans portent tous des couronnes circulaires et ils trouvent ça trop mignon.

words.notes: Konglish from English 'staff.' In Korean entertainment, 스탭 (sometimes spelled 스태프) refers to the production/support crew — managers, stylists, assistants, etc. The final consonant rendering varies: 스탭 is the more common casual spelling.

언니 literally means 'older sister' (used by a female speaker). In Korean workplace culture, especially in entertainment, female staff who are older than the artist are commonly addressed as 언니. Hwasa (a woman) calling her female staff members 언니 is natural and warm. 들 = plural, 도 = 'also/too.' 스탭 언니들 = 'the (female) staff unnies.' This tells us the staff members being referenced are women older than Hwasa.

팬 is Konglish from English 'fan.' Here 팬들 is embedded within quoted speech — the staff are saying 'the fans are all wearing crowns.' Note the absence of a particle on 팬들, which is common in casual quoted speech.
Inside the quoted speech: 'the fans ALL are wearing crowns.'
Same fandom accessory. Object particle 을 is dropped in casual speech, which is typical inside quoted speech.

words.root: 쓰다 (to wear on the head) + 고 있다 (progressive) + 더라 (retrospective)
words.notes: This is the embedded quoted speech of the staff. ~고 있다 = progressive ('are wearing'). ~더라 = retrospective ending reporting a personal observation ('I noticed that…'). The staff members are saying: 'The fans are all wearing crowns!' — sharing their own observation. 쓰고 있더라 is the direct speech being quoted before 이러면서.

words.definition: while saying this; saying things like this
words.notes: 이러다 is a contraction of 이렇게 하다 ('to do like this / to say like this'). ~(으)면서 is the simultaneous action connective: 'while doing.' 이러면서 = 'while saying things like this / while going on about it.' This is how Hwasa introduces quoted speech casually — instead of formal quotation markers, she uses 이러면서 to paraphrase what the staff were saying. Very natural spoken Korean pattern.
Positive intensifier modifying 귀여워하다.

words.root: 귀여워하다 (to find cute, to think something is cute)
words.definition: finding (it) cute; fawning over how cute (it is)
words.notes: This is the psychological verb (심리형용사) pattern: A-아/어하다. Korean descriptive verbs (adjectives) like 귀엽다 describe one's own feelings. To describe SOMEONE ELSE finding something cute, the ~아/어하다 form is required: 귀엽다 → 귀여워하다 ('to find cute / to act cute about'). ㅂ-irregular: 귀엽 → 귀여워 + 하다. The present modifier ~는 turns it into a relative clause modifying 거야: 'the thing is that they are finding it cute.' This is a crucial intermediate grammar distinction.
Same explanatory ~는 거야 pattern seen throughout. 'The thing is that they were going on about how cute the fans were.' 반말 register.

grammar.meaning: Reports a past observation of an ongoing action: 'I noticed they were V-ing'
'While saying/doing things like this' — casual way to introduce paraphrased speech
Converts a descriptive verb (adjective) into an action verb to describe someone else's feelings/reactions: 귀엽다 → 귀여워하다 ('to find cute')
Simultaneous action connective: 'while V-ing'
Casual explanatory pattern: 'the thing is that…'

sentences.en: therefore
sentences.fr: donc

words.notes: Standalone usage as a discourse filler or transition marker. When used alone like this, 그러니까 often functions as a verbal pause — the speaker is gathering their thoughts or about to make a point. It can also signal agreement ('exactly, that's what I mean'). Very common in spoken Korean as a filler, similar to English 'so…' or 'I mean…'

grammar.meaning: When used standalone, functions as a filler/pause marker while the speaker gathers thoughts, or as an agreement marker ('exactly')

sentences.en: It was so cute
sentences.fr: C'était si mignon

words.notes: Positive intensifier. Identical to sentence 61.

ㅂ-irregular adjective: 귀엽 → 귀여우 + 었 → 귀여웠 + 어. 반말 past tense. Identical form to sentence 61. Hwasa keeps returning to this expression — the repetition across multiple sentences (61, 70, 74) conveys genuine, overflowing emotion. In natural spoken Korean, such repetition is not redundant but emphatic and sincere.

grammar.meaning: Stem-final ㅂ changes to 우 before vowel suffixes

sentences.en: The weather is
sentences.fr: Le temps est

words.notes: 날씨 is a native Korean word meaning 'weather' (날 'day' + 씨, a suffix). 는 is the topic marker, signaling a topic shift: Hwasa is moving away from the crown headband discussion to talk about the weather (likely at the Hong Kong event). The sentence is a fragment — she begins a new topic but the thought continues in the next sentence. The topic marker 는 here has a contrastive or topic-shifting function: 'NOW, as for the weather…'

grammar.meaning: Topic particle used to introduce a new topic of conversation, shifting away from the previous subject

sentences.ko: 아 근데 내가 그때 전에 3월에 왔었잖아 그때는 정말 나는 최고의
sentences.en: Ah, but I came in March before then. I was really at my best back then.
sentences.fr: Ah, mais je suis venu en mars avant. J'étais vraiment à mon meilleur à l'époque.

words.notes: A natural spoken interjection signaling the speaker is recalling something or about to introduce a new thought. Here Hwasa suddenly remembers a previous visit to Hong Kong and shifts the conversation.
Contracted spoken form of 그런데. Here it functions more as 'by the way' — introducing a related but slightly tangential memory rather than a true contrast.
나 + 가 contracts to 내가. Casual 반말 first-person pronoun with subject marker.
그 ('that') + 때 ('time/moment'). A demonstrative time reference. Here it points to a previous occasion — likely a March visit to Hong Kong. Used very frequently in storytelling.

전 (前) = 'before' (Sino-Korean). 에 = time particle. 그때 전에 = 'before that time.' Can also be interpreted as 'previously' in a general sense. Note the slightly redundant/overlapping time markers (그때, 전에) — characteristic of natural unplanned speech.
3월 = 삼월 (三月), 'March.' Sino-Korean number + 월 ('month'). 에 is the time particle. Hwasa is specifying when the previous visit happened.

words.definition: I had come, you know; I came (remember?)
words.notes: Complex verb ending with multiple layers: 왔 (오 + 았, past tense) + 었 (additional past layer = past perfect / 대과거, indicating a completed action further in the past) + 잖아 (sentence ending that appeals to shared knowledge: 'you know / as you know / remember?'). The double past ~았/었었 indicates a past action that is now distanced or completed (she came in March, and that visit is now over). ~잖아 is the 반말 form of ~잖아요, used to remind the listener of something they should already know. Very common in casual conversation.

words.definition: at that time; back then (as for that time…)
words.notes: Same 그때 as above, now with the topic marker 는, which creates a contrastive nuance: 'as for THAT time (as opposed to this time/now)…' Setting up a comparison between the March visit and the current April visit.
정말 (正말 — hybrid: Sino 正 'true' + native 말 'words') = 'truly/really.' Slightly more neutral/earnest than 진짜, though both are used interchangeably in casual speech. Here it intensifies 최고의.

나 with the topic marker 는, emphasizing the speaker's personal perspective. The sentence trails off as a fragment — Hwasa starts to say she experienced 'the best…' but doesn't complete the thought in this segment.

words.root: 최고 (the best, the greatest) + 의 (possessive/modifying particle)
words.notes: 최고 (最高) = 'the highest/best' (Sino-Korean: 最 'most' + 高 'high'). 의 = possessive/attributive particle, allowing 최고 to modify a following noun: 최고의 X = 'the best X.' The sentence breaks off here — Hwasa is about to say something like '최고의 날씨' (best weather) or '최고의 경험' (best experience) but leaves it unfinished, continuing the thought in the next sentence.

grammar.meaning: Double past tense indicating a completed action further in the past, now distanced from the present: 'had V-ed'
Sentence ending appealing to shared knowledge: 'you know / as you know / remember?' — reminds the listener of something
Topic marker used to create contrast between two items or time periods
'The best N' — 최고 + possessive particle 의 forming a superlative modifier

sentences.ko: 원래도 홍콩을 좋아하긴 했지만 난 그날 진짜 최고의 홍콩 그 뭐랄까
sentences.en: I used to like Hong Kong, but I thought it was the best Hong Kong that day.
sentences.fr: J'aimais Hong Kong, mais je pensais que c'était le meilleur Hong Kong ce jour-là.

words.definition: even originally; from the start too
words.notes: 원래 (元來) = 'originally / by nature / normally' (Sino-Korean). 도 = 'also/even.' 원래도 = 'even originally / even before this.' The 도 adds emphasis: 'even before (this experience), I already liked Hong Kong.' Sets up the concession before ~지만.
을 is the object particle (after consonant). Hong Kong as the object of 좋아하다.

words.definition: I did like (it), but…; although I liked (it)…
words.notes: A layered and important construction: 좋아하다 → 좋아하기는 하다 → contracted to 좋아하긴 하다. The pattern V-기는 하다 means 'it IS the case that V / I DO V (but…)' — it acknowledges a fact while implying a contrast or reservation. ~기는 contracts to ~긴 in speech. Past tense: 했. ~지만 = 'but/although.' Full meaning: 'I DID like Hong Kong (acknowledging that), BUT…' This is a nuanced concessive-emphatic structure very common in spoken Korean.
Contracted spoken form of 나는 → 난. Very common in casual speech. The topic marker 는 creates emphasis on the speaker's personal experience.
Demonstrative time reference. 그날 = 'that day' — referring to the March visit to Hong Kong mentioned in sentence 76.
Colloquial intensifier, consistent usage.
최고 (最高) + 의. Same superlative modifier as sentence 76. 최고의 홍콩 = 'the best Hong Kong' — a creative/poetic way of saying Hong Kong was at its absolute finest that day.
Used here in an unusual but expressive way — 'the best Hong Kong' personifies the city, as if there are different versions of Hong Kong and she experienced the best one.
Here 그 functions as a filler/hesitation marker (말버릇/추임새) rather than a demonstrative. Hwasa is searching for the right word, which leads to 뭐랄까. Very common in natural spoken Korean.

words.definition: how should I put it; what would you call it
words.notes: A set hedging expression used when the speaker is searching for the right word or way to express something. Literally: 'what should (I) say?' From 뭐라고 할까 → contracted to 뭐랄까. Equivalent to English 'how do I put this…' or 'what's the word…' Very common in spoken Korean, especially during storytelling or when trying to describe an experience. The sentence trails off — Hwasa can't quite find the perfect word for how amazing Hong Kong was that day.

grammar.meaning: Acknowledges a fact with implied reservation: 'it IS the case that V (but…)' — concessive emphasis
Concessive connective ending: 'but / although'
Set expression: 'how should I put it / what's the word' — used when searching for the right expression
Spoken contraction of first-person pronoun + topic marker

sentences.ko: 그 날이 최고의 홍콩이었어 정말 날씨가 햇볕은 되게 따스한데 바람은 시원하고
sentences.en: That day was the best in Hong Kong. The weather was really warm with the sun but the wind was cool.
sentences.fr: Cette journée a été la meilleure à Hong Kong. Il faisait très chaud avec le soleil mais le vent était frais.

words.notes: 그 날 = 'that day' (the March visit). 이 is the subject particle (after consonant). Hwasa now restates and completes the thought she was searching for in sentences 76–77.
Same superlative modifier. Third time used in three consecutive sentences — shows Hwasa's strong emphasis on how perfect that day was.

이다 = copula ('to be'). Past tense: 이었. 반말 ending: 어. 최고의 홍콩이었어 = 'it was the best Hong Kong.' The creative personification continues from sentence 77 — treating 'Hong Kong' as something that can have a 'best version.'
Earnest intensifier. Transitions into the weather description that justifies the 'best Hong Kong' claim.
날씨 = 'weather' (native Korean). 가 = subject particle (after vowel). Introduces the weather as the reason why that day was the best.

words.definition: as for the sunlight; the sun (contrastive topic)
words.notes: 햇볕 = 햇 (from 해, 'sun,' with the possessive ㅅ sai-siot) + 볕 ('sunshine/warmth'). A native Korean compound meaning 'sunlight/sunshine.' 은 is the topic marker, used here contrastively: 'as for the SUNLIGHT (it was warm), but as for the WIND (it was cool).' This contrastive topic marking is a hallmark of elegant Korean description.

Colloquial intensifier, originally from 되다 ('to become') + 게 (adverbializer). In casual spoken Korean, 되게 is widely used as an alternative to 매우/아주/너무 meaning 'very/really.' It is informal and characteristic of everyday speech. More casual than 매우 or 상당히.

words.definition: it's warm, but…; it was warm, and…
words.notes: 따스하다 is a softer/more poetic variant of 따뜻하다 ('to be warm'). Both mean 'warm,' but 따스하다 has a gentler, more lyrical feel — slightly literary or dialectal. ~(으)ㄴ데 is the contrast/background connective for adjectives: 'it's warm, BUT (the wind is cool).' This sets up the pleasant contrast in the weather description.

바람 = 'wind' (native Korean). 은 is the contrastive topic marker, paired with 햇볕은 above: 'the sunlight was warm BUT the wind was cool.' This parallel structure (X은 A, Y은 B) is a beautiful and natural Korean way to describe contrasting qualities.

시원하다 = 'to be cool/refreshing.' A versatile adjective — can describe temperature (cool breeze), taste (refreshing soup), or even emotional relief (시원하다 after resolving a problem). Here it describes the pleasant cool wind. ~고 connects to the continuing description (sentence 79 adds '안 습해'). The overall weather portrait: warm sun + cool wind + not humid = perfect.

grammar.pattern: X은/는 A, Y은/는 B (contrastive topic parallel structure)
grammar.meaning: Using the topic marker on two items to highlight their contrasting qualities: 'as for X, it's A; as for Y, it's B'
Background/contrast connective attached to adjective stems: 'it's A, but…'
Copula 'to be' in past tense casual form

sentences.en: But it's not humid
sentences.fr: Mais ce n'est pas humide

words.notes: Here 근데 functions more as an additive connector ('and on top of that') rather than a true contrast. Hwasa is adding another positive point about the weather: warm sun + cool breeze + AND it's not humid.
Short-form negation before the adjective 습하다.

습하다 = 'to be humid/damp.' Sino-Korean: 습 (濕, 'moisture/damp') + 하다. Conjugation: 습하 + 여 → 습해 (하 + 여 contracts to 해). 반말 sentence ending. 안 습해 = 'it's not humid.' This completes the perfect weather trifecta Hwasa is describing: warm sunshine, cool breeze, no humidity. Note: Hong Kong is famously humid in summer, so the lack of humidity in March would be noteworthy.

grammar.meaning: Negating a descriptive verb/adjective with the short-form negation 안

sentences.ko: 근데 그 날씨가 한국이 겨울일때부터 한 3월까지가 홍콩에 되게 좋다고 하더라고 안 습하고
sentences.en: However, although the weather is said to be very good in Hong Kong from the time it is winter in Korea until mid-March, it is not humid.
sentences.fr: Cependant, même si l'on dit que le temps est très beau à Hong Kong depuis l'hiver en Corée jusqu'à la mi-mars, il n'est pas humide.

words.notes: Here functioning as a transitional connector — Hwasa is adding background information she learned about Hong Kong's climate.

Functions as a determiner modifying 날씨 ('that weather / the weather'), softly referring to the weather phenomenon she experienced and is about to explain. Could also carry a slight filler quality as she formulates a complex sentence.
날씨 = 'weather' (native Korean). 가 = subject particle (after vowel). The weather is the subject of the overall sentence — specifically, the good weather period that people told her about.
한국 (韓國) = 'Korea / South Korea.' 이 = subject particle (after consonant). Korea is the subject within the embedded time clause: 한국이 겨울일 때 = 'when it is winter in Korea.'

A complex time phrase built in layers: 겨울 = 'winter' (native Korean). 이다 = copula ('to be'). ~(으)ㄹ 때 = 'when (it is)' — the future/general modifier ㄹ is used because this describes a recurring/habitual condition, not a one-time past event. 부터 = 'from' (starting-point particle). Full: 'from the time when (Korea) is winter.' This is the starting point of the time range.
Approximation adverb placed before numbers or time expressions. 한 3월 = 'around March / about March.' More casual than 약 (約). Very common in spoken Korean for softening precision.

3월 = 삼월 (三月), 'March.' 까지 = 'until/up to' (endpoint particle). 가 = subject particle. The particle stacking 까지가 is natural in Korean — 까지 marks the endpoint of the time range, then 가 marks the entire range (겨울일때부터 한 3월까지) as the grammatical subject of 좋다. The structure is: '[from winter] [until about March] = [that period] is good (in Hong Kong).'
에 = location particle. Specifies where the weather is good during that period.
Colloquial intensifier, same as in sentence 78. Modifies 좋다. More casual than 매우 or 아주.

좋다 = 'to be good.' ~다고 is the indirect quotation particle for declarative statements. It marks the content of what someone told Hwasa: '(people say) that the weather is really good.' The quotation verb 하다 follows as 하더라고.

words.definition: people said / I heard (that); they told me (that)
words.notes: 하다 here is the quotation verb ('to say'). ~더라고(요) is a compound ending: ~더 (retrospective, recalling a past experience) + ~라고 (quotation). Together, ~더라고 means 'I recall that (someone) said…' or 'they told me (and I'm reporting it now).' This is different from plain ~더라 (reporting one's own observation) — ~더라고 reports what OTHERS said as recalled by the speaker. It's 반말 register; the polite form is 하더라고요. Key distinction for learners: ~더라 = 'I personally experienced/noticed that…' vs. ~다고 하더라고 = 'I recall people saying that…'
Short-form negation before 습하다. Same structure as sentence 79.

습하다 = 'to be humid' (Sino-Korean: 濕 'damp' + 하다). The connective ~고 links this to further description (possibly continuing in the next sentence or trailing off). 안 습하고 = 'it's not humid, and…' This elaborates on WHY the weather is good — adding 'not humid' as an additional quality to the warm sun and cool breeze described in sentences 78–79. The trailing ~고 leaves the list open, as if there may be more to say.

grammar.meaning: Hearsay retrospective: 'I recall (someone) saying that…' — reports what others told the speaker
Time clause: 'when / at the time when' — with the general/future modifier for habitual conditions
Range pattern: 'from ~ until ~' — marks the starting point and endpoint of a period
Multiple particles on one noun phrase: 까지 (endpoint) + 가 (subject). The entire range becomes the grammatical subject.
~더라 reports one's OWN past observation; ~더라고 (from ~다고 하더라) reports what OTHERS said as recalled by the speaker. Key distinction.
Adverb meaning 'about/approximately' placed before quantities or time expressions

sentences.ko: 맞아 맞아 11월에서 3월이 되게 홍콩이 너무 좋은 날씨라는 거야
sentences.en: That's right, the weather in Hong Kong is really nice from November to March.
sentences.fr: C'est vrai, le climat à Hong Kong est vraiment agréable de novembre à mars.

words.notes: 맞다 = 'to be correct/right.' 맞아 is the 반말 conjugation (맞 + 아). Repeating it twice (맞아 맞아) is a very natural spoken pattern expressing enthusiastic agreement — 'yes yes, exactly!' Hwasa is confirming information, likely responding to something a staff member or she herself recalled about Hong Kong's climate.

11월 = 십일월 (十一月), 'November.' 에서 here functions as a starting-point particle meaning 'from,' synonymous with 부터 in this time-range context. The pattern N에서 N까지 = 'from N to N' is commonly used for ranges. Note: 에서 more often marks the location of an action, but with time/number ranges it can mean 'from.' Compare with 부터…까지 in sentence 80.

words.definition: March (endpoint, as part of the subject)
words.notes: 3월 = 삼월 (三月), 'March.' The 이 subject marker here is slightly unusual — in natural spoken Korean, the sentence structure is somewhat loose. The range '11월에서 3월' functions as a time frame within which Hong Kong's weather is good. The 이 may be attaching to the endpoint or serving a structural role in the informal syntax.
Same colloquial intensifier as in sentences 78 and 80. Modifies 좋은.

홍콩 = 'Hong Kong.' 이 = subject particle (after consonant). In this loose spoken structure, 홍콩이 identifies the place whose weather is being described. Note the sentence has somewhat scrambled word order compared to formal writing — this is normal in casual speech.
Positive intensifier, consistent colloquial usage throughout.
~(으)ㄴ is the adjective modifier ending. 좋은 날씨 = 'good/nice weather.'

words.root: 날씨 (weather) + 이라는 (that is called; which is)
words.definition: weather that is (described as); what they call good weather
words.notes: ~(이)라는 is a quotative modifier from ~(이)라고 하는, meaning 'that is called / which is said to be / that is.' It combines the copula quotation ~(이)라고 with the modifier 하는, contracted to ~(이)라는. Here: 좋은 날씨라는 거야 = 'the thing is that it's (what they call) good weather.' This adds a layer of reported/explanatory framing.

Same explanatory ~는/~라는 거야 pattern seen throughout. 좋은 날씨라는 거야 = 'the thing is, it's (said to be) really nice weather.' 반말 register. This wraps up Hwasa's climate explanation with a conclusive explanatory tone.

grammar.meaning: 'From N to N' — 에서 marks the starting point of a range (time or space), parallel to 부터…까지
Contracted from ~(이)라고 하는: 'that is called / which is said to be / that is'
Explanatory pattern with quotative: 'the thing is that it's…' / 'what I mean is it's…'

sentences.ko: 오 그랬는데 이번에는 좀 습하긴 했는데 습한데 너무 좋았어
sentences.en: Oh, I did, but it was a little humid this time, but it was so nice to be humid.
sentences.fr: Oh, je l'ai fait, mais c'était un peu humide cette fois, mais c'était tellement agréable d'être humide.

words.notes: A natural interjection expressing mild surprise or acknowledgment. Hwasa is transitioning from the general climate knowledge to her actual experience this time.

words.root: 그렇다 (to be so, to be like that)
words.definition: it was like that, but…; that was the case, however…
words.notes: 그렇다 = 'to be so/like that.' Irregular conjugation: 그렇 + 았 → 그랬 (ㅎ-irregular: ㅎ drops and vowels merge). ~는데 = background/contrast connective. 그랬는데 = 'it was like that (in March), but (this time)…' Acknowledges the previous point before introducing a contrast.
