words.root: 이번 (this time) + 에 (time particle) + 는 (contrastive topic marker)
words.notes: 이번 = 'this time / this occasion.' 에 = time particle. 는 = contrastive topic marker, explicitly contrasting the current April visit with the previous March visit. The stacking 에는 is very common: the time particle 에 marks when, and 는 adds the contrastive nuance.
Contracted spoken form of 조금 ('a little'). Softens the statement: 'a BIT humid.' Very common in casual speech. Also used as a politeness softener in requests (좀 해주세요).

Same V-기는 하다 pattern as in sentence 77 (좋아하긴 했지만). 습하기는 했다 → contracted to 습하긴 했다. The pattern acknowledges a fact while implying a reservation or contrast: 'it WAS humid, I'll grant that, BUT…' Past tense 했 + ~는데 (background/contrast). This is Hwasa conceding the humidity while setting up that it was still enjoyable.

습하다 + ~(으)ㄴ데 (adjective contrast connective). Hwasa restates 'it's humid BUT…' — this slight repetition/rephrasing (습하긴 했는데 → 습한데) is characteristic of natural unplanned speech where the speaker refines their thought mid-sentence. The second 습한데 simplifies the construction before delivering the main point.
Positive intensifier.

words.definition: it was good; it was great
words.notes: Past tense 반말 form. The emotional payoff of the concessive structure: despite the humidity, the experience was wonderful. The whole sentence structure — concession → concession restatement → positive conclusion — is very natural in spoken Korean storytelling.

grammar.meaning: Concessive-emphatic: 'it IS/WAS the case that V/A (but…)' — acknowledges a fact before contrasting
'It is A, but…' — contrast/background connective for descriptive verbs
'This time (as opposed to before)' — 에 (time) + 는 (contrastive topic) stacking
When a stem ending in ㅎ meets a vowel suffix, the ㅎ drops and vowels may merge: 그렇 + 았 → 그랬
Speaker restates or simplifies a construction mid-sentence — 습하긴 했는데 → 습한데. Common in unplanned spoken Korean.

sentences.ko: 그러니까 나도 우기가 있는지 몰랐어 홍콩이
sentences.en: So I didn't know there was a rainy season in Hong Kong either.
sentences.fr: Donc je ne savais pas non plus qu'il y avait une saison des pluies à Hong Kong.

words.definition: so; I mean; the thing is
words.notes: Conjunction introducing an explanatory aside. Hwasa is saying 'the thing is, I didn't even know Hong Kong had a rainy season.'

words.definition: I also; even I; me too
words.notes: 나 = casual first-person pronoun. 도 = 'also/even.' 나도 = 'even I / I also (didn't know).' The 도 implies others might not have known either, or that it's surprising that she herself didn't know.
우기 (雨期) = 'rainy season' (Sino-Korean: 雨 'rain' + 期 'period/season'). The opposite is 건기 (乾期, 'dry season'). 가 = subject particle (after vowel). 우기가 있다 = 'there is a rainy season.'

words.definition: whether there is; if there exists
words.notes: 있다 = 'to exist/be.' ~는지 creates an indirect question or embedded clause: 'whether/if.' 우기가 있는지 = 'whether there is a rainy season.' When combined with 모르다, it means 'didn't know whether/that there was a rainy season.' The pattern V-는지 모르다 = 'to not know if/that V.'
모르다 = 'to not know.' 르-irregular conjugation in past tense: 모르 + 았 → 몰랐 (ㄹ doubles, ㅡ drops). 반말 ending 어. 몰랐어 = 'I didn't know.' This is the main predicate of the sentence.

Placed at the end of the sentence as an afterthought/postposition (도치). The natural formal order would be 홍콩이 우기가 있는지 몰랐어, but Hwasa adds 홍콩이 at the end to clarify what she's talking about. This subject postposition is a hallmark of casual spoken Korean, same phenomenon as in sentence 51 (컨디션이). It functions like an English afterthought: 'I didn't know there was a rainy season — Hong Kong, I mean.'

grammar.meaning: 'To not know whether/that V' — indirect question embedded with the verb of not knowing
Placing the subject at the end of the sentence as an afterthought or clarification — characteristic of spoken Korean
모르 + 았 → 몰랐: ㄹ doubles and ㅡ drops before 아/어

sentences.ko: 근데 생각해보니까 아 맞아 내가 홍콩 올 때마다 뭔가 좀 습한 느낌이 있었는데 그게 우기였구나
sentences.en: But when I thought about it, oh yeah, every time I came to Hong Kong, it felt a bit humid, and that was during the rainy season.
sentences.fr: Mais quand j'y pensais, oh oui, à chaque fois que je venais à Hong Kong, c'était un peu humide, et c'était pendant la saison des pluies.

words.notes: Contracted form of 그런데. Here it introduces a realization — 'but (when I think about it)…'

words.definition: when I thought about it; now that I think about it
words.notes: A layered construction: 생각하다 = 'to think' (생각 = 'thought,' Sino-Korean 想覺 + 하다). V-아/어 보다 = auxiliary verb meaning 'to try V-ing.' 생각해 보다 = 'to try thinking about it / to think it over.' ~(으)니까 in the discovery sense: 'when I did X, I realized that…' Full meaning: 'when I thought about it (I realized)…' This is a very natural storytelling phrase — the speaker introduces a moment of retrospective realization.
Interjection of realization. Hwasa is dramatizing the moment of her epiphany: 'ah, right!'
맞아 = 'that's right!' Here it signals a self-directed realization: 'oh, that's right (I remember now)!' Same form as sentence 81 but used reflexively rather than in agreement with someone else.
Contracted form of 나 + 가. Subject of the time clause: 'every time I come to Hong Kong.'
Used here without a particle — the destination particle 에 is dropped in casual speech. 홍콩 (에) 오다 = 'to come to Hong Kong.'

words.definition: every time I come; whenever I come
words.notes: A very useful compound pattern: V-(으)ㄹ 때 = 'when one V-s' (general/habitual). 마다 = 'every/each.' V-(으)ㄹ 때마다 = 'every time one V-s / whenever one V-s.' 올 때마다 = 'every time I come.' The prospective modifier ㄹ is used because this describes a recurring pattern, not a single past event.

Contracted from 무엇인가 ('something or other'). In casual spoken Korean, 뭔가 is frequently used as a vague hedging adverb meaning 'somehow / sort of / in some way.' Here: 뭔가 좀 습한 느낌 = 'a sort of somewhat humid feeling.' It softens the description, making it less definitive — she had a vague sense of humidity but couldn't quite put her finger on it at the time.
Contracted form of 조금. Softens the adjective 습한: 'a bit humid.' Combined with 뭔가, creates a doubly hedged expression: 'sort of a bit humid.'
습하다 + ~(으)ㄴ (adjective modifier). 습한 느낌 = 'a humid feeling/sense.'
느낌 is derived from 느끼다 ('to feel') + ~(으)ㅁ (nominalizer) → 느낌 = 'a feeling/impression.' 이 = subject particle. 습한 느낌이 있었다 = 'there was a humid feeling/impression.'

words.definition: there was, and…; there had been, but…
words.notes: 있다 = 'to exist.' Past tense: 있었. ~는데 = background/setup connective. 습한 느낌이 있었는데 = 'there had been a humid feeling, and (now I realize)…' Sets up the realization that follows.
Contracted from 그것이 → 그게. Refers back to the humid feeling she always noticed: 'that (humidity I felt) was…'

words.definition: it was the rainy season! (I now realize)
words.notes: 우기 (雨期) = 'rainy season.' 이다 = copula. 이었 = past copula. ~구나 is the exclamatory ending expressing a new realization or discovery: 'oh, so it was…!' / 'I see now that it was…!' This is a key grammar point: ~구나/~는구나 expresses the speaker's moment of realization or newfound understanding. It is 반말 register; the polite form would be ~군요. The sentence beautifully captures Hwasa's eureka moment: she always felt the humidity but only now connects it to the rainy season. ~구나 is the perfect ending for this discovery.

grammar.meaning: Auxiliary verb meaning 'to try doing V' — here 생각해 보다 = 'to think it over / to try thinking about it'
'When I tried V-ing, I found/realized that…' — combines the auxiliary 보다 with the discovery connective ~(으)니까
'Every time V / whenever V' — habitual time clause with 마다 for repetition
Exclamatory realization ending with past copula: 'oh, so it was…!' — expresses the speaker's newfound understanding
Exclamatory ending expressing realization or discovery: 'oh, I see! / so that's what it was!'
Spoken contraction of demonstrative pronoun + subject particle
In sentence 83, 홍콩이 was postposed as an afterthought; in sentence 84, Hwasa integrates it properly into the time clause, showing how speakers self-correct across sentences

sentences.ko: 아 오늘도 비교적 안 습한 거야?
sentences.en: Oh, it's relatively humid today too?
sentences.fr: Oh, il fait relativement humide aujourd'hui aussi ?

words.notes: Interjection of mild surprise or interest. Hwasa is reacting to new information — possibly someone telling her about today's humidity level.
오늘 = 'today.' 도 = 'also/too.' 오늘도 = 'today also,' implying that today is another day with the same condition (not humid), connecting to the earlier discussion about Hong Kong's dry-season weather.

비교 (比較) = 'comparison' (Sino-Korean) + 적 (的) = adverbial suffix meaning '-ly / -ically.' 비교적 = 'relatively/comparatively.' A somewhat formal/educated adverb that stands out in Hwasa's otherwise casual speech — she's qualifying the statement: it's not completely dry, but RELATIVELY not humid.
Short-form negation before the adjective 습하다.
습하다 + ~(으)ㄴ (adjective modifier). 안 습한 = 'not humid.' Here modifying the bound noun 거 (것).

Same ~(으)ㄴ/는 거야 pattern, but with rising intonation making it a question. 안 습한 거야? = 'Is it (the case that it's) not humid?' In spoken Korean, statements and questions in 반말 are distinguished purely by intonation — the form 거야 can be either declarative or interrogative. This is a key listening skill for learners.

grammar.meaning: Explanatory pattern as a question (반말): 'is it that…?' — distinguished from the declarative form by rising intonation alone
Short-form negation with adjective: 'not A'
In 반말/해체, questions and statements share the same grammatical form — only rising intonation distinguishes them

sentences.en: So please invite me again. It was so fun.
sentences.fr: Alors s'il vous plaît, invitez-moi à nouveau. C'était tellement amusant.

words.notes: A further colloquial contraction of 그러니까 → 그니까. While 그러니까 is already casual, 그니까 is even more reduced and characteristic of very relaxed speech. This double contraction (그러니까 → 그니까) parallels 그런데 → 근데. Hwasa uses this to casually transition to a request.
Native Korean adverb meaning 'again/once more.' 또 초대해줘 = 'invite me again.' Expresses Hwasa's desire to return — she enjoyed the Hong Kong event so much she wants to be invited back.

words.root: 초대하다 (to invite) + ~아/어 주다 (to do for someone)
words.breakdown: 초대 + 하 + 여 + 주 + 어 → 초대해줘
words.definition: invite me (please); do me the favor of inviting me
words.notes: 초대 (招待) = 'invitation' (Sino-Korean) + 하다 = 'to invite.' V-아/어 주다 is the benefactive auxiliary: 'to do V for someone's benefit.' 초대해 주다 = 'to invite (for my benefit).' In 반말, 주어 → 줘. 초대해줘 = 'invite me (please)!' — a casual but heartfelt request. Hwasa is likely speaking to the event organizers or generally expressing her wish to return. Note: even in 반말, ~아/어 줘 can sound like a polite request depending on tone.
Positive intensifier, consistent usage.

words.definition: it was fun; it was a great time
words.notes: 재미있다 = 재미 ('fun/interest') + 있다 ('to exist'). In casual speech and writing, 재미있다 contracts to 재밌다 (재미있 → 재밌). Past tense: 재밌 + 었 + 어 = 재밌었어. This contraction is universally understood and used in informal contexts. The formal/full form 재미있었어 is also correct but less common in speech. Hwasa is justifying her request: 'invite me again — it was SO fun!'

grammar.meaning: 'To do V for someone's benefit' — when used as a request, it means 'please do V (for me)'
Further casual contraction of the conjunction 그러니까
Common spoken/informal contraction of 재미있다 → 재밌다

sentences.en: It was so much fun
sentences.fr: C'était tellement amusant

words.notes: Positive intensifier. Identical to the previous sentence — Hwasa repeats the entire phrase for emphasis.

words.definition: it was fun; it was a blast
words.notes: Same contracted form as sentence 86. The verbatim repetition of 너무 재밌었어 from the previous sentence is a natural spoken emphasis strategy — Hwasa is underlining just how much she enjoyed the Hong Kong event. In Korean conversation, repeating a phrase like this is not redundant but emotionally sincere, conveying genuine enthusiasm.

grammar.meaning: Repeating an entire phrase across sentences to convey sincerity and emotional intensity — common in spoken Korean

sentences.ko: 오 장모철에 감자칩 꺼내면 바로 종이처럼 눅눅해진다고?
sentences.en: Oh, when you take out potato chips during the mother-in-law season, they immediately become soggy like paper?
sentences.fr: Oh, quand on sort des chips pendant la saison des belles-mères, elles deviennent immédiatement détrempées comme du papier ?

words.notes: Interjection of surprise. Hwasa is reacting to someone's description of Hong Kong's rainy-season humidity with amazement.

This is almost certainly 장마철 (장마 + 철) — the audio transcription renders it as 장모철, but 장마철 is the correct term. 장마 (長霖) = 'monsoon/prolonged rainy period' (Sino-Korean: 長 'long' + 霖 'continuous rain'). 철 = 'season/period' (e.g., 겨울철 'winter season,' 장마철 'monsoon season'). 에 = time particle. The 아/오 vowel confusion is a common transcription artifact in casual speech. Note: the English/French translations render this as 'mother-in-law season' (장모 = 'mother-in-law'), which is a mistranslation based on the transcription error. The correct meaning is 'rainy/monsoon season.' Korea's 장마철 typically runs June–July; Hong Kong's rainy season is roughly April–September.

감자 = 'potato' (native Korean). 칩 = Konglish from English 'chip.' 감자칩 = 'potato chip(s).' The soggy-chips example is a classic and universally understood illustration that Koreans use to convey extreme humidity — everyone knows the frustration of chips going soft during 장마철.

words.root: 꺼내다 (to take out, to pull out)
words.definition: if you take (them) out; when you take (them) out
words.notes: 꺼내다 = 'to take out / pull out / bring out.' From 꺼내다 (related to 껍데기 'shell/cover' — taking something out from inside). ~(으)면 = conditional 'if/when.' 꺼내면 = 'if/when you take them out (of the bag).' The conditional here describes a general/habitual situation: 'whenever you take out chips (during the rainy season), they get soggy.'

바로 has multiple meanings: 'right away,' 'directly,' 'correctly,' 'right (next to).' Here it means 'immediately/instantly' — the chips become soggy the moment you open the bag. Emphasizes how extreme the humidity is.

종이 = 'paper' (native Korean). 처럼 = comparison particle meaning 'like / as if.' 종이처럼 = 'like paper.' The simile describes chips losing all their crunch and becoming flat and limp like a piece of paper — a vivid image of humidity's effect. 처럼 is interchangeable with 같이 in most contexts, though 처럼 is slightly more formal/literary.

words.root: 눅눅하다 (to be damp, soggy, moist) + ~아/어지다 (to become) + ~다고 (quotation, questioning)
words.definition: they become soggy, you say?; they get damp (really)?
words.notes: A rich, multi-layered ending: 눅눅하다 = 'to be damp/soggy/moist' — an expressive/mimetic (의태어-adjacent) adjective describing the unpleasant soft dampness of things that should be crispy. A-아/어지다 = inchoative pattern meaning 'to become A': 눅눅해지다 = 'to become soggy/damp.' Present tense declarative: 눅눅해진다 (~ㄴ/는다 is the plain/diary present tense form). ~다고? = quotative particle used as a question — Hwasa is echoing/quoting what someone just told her and expressing disbelief: 'they become soggy like paper, you say?!' This echo-question with ~다고? is extremely common in Korean conversation: it quotes the other person's statement back as a surprised question. 반말 register.

grammar.meaning: Attaches to adjective stems to express change of state: 'to become A'
Quoting someone else's statement back as a surprised question: 'you're saying that…?!' / 'really?!'
'If/when V' — here describing a general/habitual condition rather than a one-time hypothetical
'Like N / as if N' — comparison/simile particle
Plain/diary style present tense for action verbs, used inside quotations and in written/reported speech: V-ㄴ다/는다

sentences.ko: 이런 홍콩 날씨를 좋아한다고 말한 사람은 니가 처음이야
sentences.en: You are the first person to say that they like Hong Kong weather like this.
sentences.fr: Vous êtes la première personne à dire qu'elle aime ce climat à Hong Kong.

words.notes: Pre-noun form used to modify the following noun. Shortened from 이러한. Very common in spoken Korean.
Phonetic rendering of 'Hong Kong' in Korean. Technically a Sino-foreign loanword, not Konglish.

words.definition: weather (as the object of the verb 좋아하다)
words.notes: 를 is the object-marking particle used after vowel-ending nouns. 을 is used after consonant-ending nouns.

words.breakdown: 좋아하 + ㄴ다 (plain-form present declarative) + 고 (quotation particle)
words.notes: Indirect quotation form: Verb stem + ㄴ다고 for action verbs in present tense. This is the ~(ㄴ/는)다고 pattern used for reported/indirect speech. The ㄴ다 is the plain-style (해라체) declarative ending required inside quotation constructions.
Past tense modifier (관형형) that modifies the following noun 사람. ~(으)ㄴ after an action verb indicates a completed action modifying a noun.

words.definition: the person (who said…), as for the person
words.notes: 은 is the topic-marking particle after a consonant-ending noun. Here it sets up 사람 as the topic of the sentence, contrasting with 니가 처음이야.

words.breakdown: 니 (colloquial form of 네/너) + 가 (subject particle)
words.notes: In spoken Korean, 네가 ('you' + subject particle) is often pronounced and written as 니가 to distinguish it from 내가 ('I' + subject particle). This is 반말 (casual speech), indicating closeness with the listener. Standard written form is 네가.

words.breakdown: 처음 + 이 (copula 이다) + 야 (반말 declarative ending)
words.notes: 이야 is the 반말 (casual) present declarative form of the copula 이다, used after a consonant-ending noun. After vowel-ending nouns it becomes ~야. The speech level is casual/intimate (반말).

grammar.meaning: Indirect quotation for declarative statements — 'that (someone) says/said…'
Past tense modifier for action verbs — describes a noun with a completed action
Casual declarative copula ending — 'is/am/are'
Sets up a topic ('the person who said X') and makes a comment about it ('is you, the first')

sentences.en: No, it was really good
sentences.fr: Non, c'était vraiment bien

words.notes: 반말 form of 아니다. Used to deny or contradict what someone else said. In 해요체 it would be 아니에요. Here Hwasa is casually pushing back on the previous speaker's implication.
Very common colloquial intensifier. Can function as a noun ('the real thing') or adverb ('really'). Extremely frequent in spoken Korean, especially casual speech. Similar to 정말 but more colloquial.

words.breakdown: 좋 + 았 (past tense) + 어 (반말 declarative ending)
words.notes: Past tense 반말 form of 좋다. The 았 is the past tense marker selected because the stem vowel 좋 contains ㅗ (bright vowel), triggering 았 rather than 었 (vowel harmony). 해요체 form would be 좋았어요.

grammar.meaning: Casual past tense declarative ending — 'did / was'
Casual-register denial — 'No / That's not true'

sentences.ko: 아 7월에는 습기가 많구나 그럴 수도 있겠다
sentences.en: Oh, it might be humid in July.
sentences.fr: Oh, il pourrait faire humide en juillet.

words.definition: Oh, ah — expressing realization or acknowledgement
words.notes: Very common interjection. Here it signals that Hwasa is just now understanding or considering new information (the humidity in July).

words.definition: in July (as for July / as a contrasted topic)
words.notes: 에 marks the time reference ('in July'). The added 는 creates a contrastive nuance — 'in July specifically (as opposed to other months)'. This 에는 stacking is very natural in Korean and a key intermediate skill.
Sino-Korean word: 습(濕) = wet/damp + 기(氣) = air/energy. 가 is the subject particle used after vowel-ending nouns.

words.root: 많다 (to be many, to be a lot)
words.definition: there's a lot (of humidity)! / it's quite humid!
words.notes: ~구나 is a 반말 exclamatory ending expressing new realization or discovery ('Oh, so it's…!'). Used in the 해라체 (plain) speech level. For adjectives: stem + 구나. For action verbs: stem + 는구나. This is different from ~군요 (해요체 equivalent).

words.root: 그러하다 / 그렇다 (to be so, to be like that)
words.breakdown: 그러 (stem of 그러하다) + ㄹ (future/prospective adnominal ending)
words.definition: that being the case, it being so
words.notes: 그럴 is the contracted future modifier form of 그렇다. Here it modifies 수 in the pattern 그럴 수도 있다 ('it could be so'). 그렇다 is an irregular ㅎ-adjective: 그렇 → 그러 before vowel-initial suffixes.

words.definition: the possibility also / even the possibility
words.notes: 수 is a bound noun (의존 명사) meaning 'way/means/possibility' — it cannot stand alone and must follow a modifier. 도 ('also/even') adds the nuance of concession: 'it could even be the case that…'.

words.definition: there could be, it might be
words.notes: ~겠다 expresses the speaker's conjecture, supposition, or mild future intention. Here it means 'I suppose it could be.' The plain ending ~다 (해라체) is used because Hwasa is speaking to herself / thinking aloud. Combined: 그럴 수도 있겠다 = 'I suppose that could be the case.'

grammar.meaning: Exclamatory ending expressing new realization or discovery — 'Oh, so it is…!'
Expression of possibility with concessive nuance — 'it could (also) be that…'
Conjecture or supposition — 'I suppose / it seems like / probably'
Marks a time or place with contrastive or topicalizing nuance — 'as for (in) X'

sentences.ko: 와이파이가 안 좋다고? 여기선 완전 좋은데?
sentences.en: Wi-Fi is bad? It's really good here, right?
sentences.fr: Le Wi-Fi est mauvais ? C'est vraiment bien ici, non ?

words.notes: Konglish loanword from English 'Wi-Fi'. Pronounced 와이파이 [wa-i-pa-i]. Very commonly used in everyday Korean. 가 is the subject particle after vowel-ending nouns.
Short-form negation placed directly before the verb/adjective. This is the 'short negation' (단형 부정) as opposed to the ~지 않다 long form. Very common in casual spoken Korean.

words.breakdown: 좋 + 다고 (indirect quotation particle for adjectives)
words.definition: that it's good / (you're saying) it's not good?
words.notes: Indirect quotation for adjective declaratives: stem + 다고. Here 안 좋다고? is quoting someone else's claim with a questioning tone — 'Are you saying the Wi-Fi isn't good?' This is a common spoken pattern for expressing surprise at what someone said.

words.breakdown: 여기 + 서 (location particle 에서) + ㄴ (는, contrastive topic particle)
words.notes: 여기서 = 여기에서 ('at here / in this place') — the 에 is commonly dropped in speech. 선 = 서 + 는 (contraction of the topic particle). The 는 adds contrast: 'HERE (as opposed to where you are), it's great.' This double contraction (에서 → 서, 서는 → 선) is very common in spoken Korean.

Sino-Korean word (完全) originally meaning 'complete/perfect.' In colloquial Korean it's used as a slang intensifier meaning 'totally/super,' especially popular among younger speakers. Similar to 진짜 or 정말 but more emphatic and casual.

words.definition: it's good though / it's good, but…
words.notes: ~(으)ㄴ데 after adjectives provides background information, contrast, or mild objection. With rising intonation (indicated by ?) it becomes a tag-question-like expression: 'it's good here though?' / 'but it's great here?' For action verbs the form would be ~는데.

grammar.meaning: Repeats someone else's statement as a question to express surprise or seek confirmation — '(You're saying) …?'
Negates the following predicate — 'not …'
Provides background, contrast, or mild objection — 'but / though / and (so)'
Contracted location particle with contrastive topic — 'at (this place), in contrast…'

sentences.en: I couldn't see much this time.
sentences.fr: Je ne pouvais pas voir grand-chose cette fois.

words.breakdown: 이번 + 에 (time particle) + ㄴ (는, topic/contrast particle, contracted)
words.definition: this time (in contrast to other times)
words.notes: 이번에는 → 이번엔 is a very common spoken contraction. The 는 adds contrastive nuance: 'THIS time (unlike last time).' Given the context, Hwasa is comparing this Hong Kong trip to her previous March visit.

구경 means 'viewing/watching/looking around' and is often used in the pattern 구경하다 ('to go sightseeing / to look around'). Here 구경을 하다 is split with the object particle, and the 하다 portion appears as 못했어. 을 is the object particle after consonant-ending nouns.
Adverbial form of 많다. Here it combines with the negation 못 to mean 'couldn't do much (sightseeing).' The word order 많이 못했어 is natural in spoken Korean.

words.breakdown: 못 (inability negation) + 하 (하다, to do) + 았 (past tense) + 어 (반말 declarative ending)
words.definition: couldn't do, was unable to do
words.notes: 못 is the negation of ability ('cannot'), as opposed to 안 which is negation of volition ('do not'). 못했어 is the 반말 past tense of 못하다. Here it completes 구경을 많이 못했어 = 'couldn't do much sightseeing.' 해요체 would be 못했어요.

grammar.meaning: Expresses inability — 'cannot / couldn't do'
Contracted time particle with contrastive topic — 'this time (as opposed to another time)'
Couldn't do much of (something) — negation combined with degree adverb

sentences.ko: 저번에 3월 때처럼 막 그렇게 돌아다니진 못했고 어제는
sentences.en: I couldn't walk around like I did last time in March, and yesterday
sentences.fr: Je ne pouvais pas me promener comme je l'ai fait la dernière fois en mars et hier

words.notes: 저번 is a colloquial/spoken form of 지난번 ('last time'). Very common in casual speech. Hwasa is referring to her previous Hong Kong visit in March 2026.
Sino-Korean number system for months: 일월 (January) through 십이월 (December). 삼월 = third month = March.

words.definition: like (that) time, as (it was) at that time
words.notes: 때 is a bound-ish noun meaning 'time/when.' 처럼 is a comparative particle meaning 'like/as.' Together: 3월 때처럼 = 'like the time in March.' 처럼 is interchangeable with 같이 in many contexts.

words.definition: freely, all over the place, just (doing something without restraint)
words.notes: Highly colloquial adverb meaning 'just / recklessly / without thinking / all over the place.' Very characteristic of casual spoken Korean. Here it conveys 'just walking around freely' — an unstructured, carefree wandering. One of those words that's hard to translate directly but adds vivid color to speech.

words.root: 그렇다 (to be so, to be like that)
words.notes: Adverbial form of 그렇다 (ㅎ-irregular: 그렇 → 그러 before some endings, but 그렇게 is a fixed form). Here it references the manner of her previous March wandering: 'like that / in that way.'

words.root: 돌아다니다 (to walk around, to wander about)
words.breakdown: 돌아다니 + 지 (nominalizing/negation auxiliary) + ㄴ (는, topic/contrast particle, contracted)
words.definition: as for walking around (couldn't do it)
words.notes: 돌아다니다 is a compound verb: 돌아 (돌다, to turn) + 다니다 (to go around/attend). ~지는 → ~진 is a contraction where 는 adds contrastive emphasis to the negation: 'walking around, (that specifically) I couldn't do.' The ~지(는) 못하다 pattern is the long-form inability negation with added emphasis.
~고 is a connective ending meaning 'and' or 'and then,' linking two clauses. 못했고 = 'couldn't do (that), and…' The sentence trails off as Hwasa transitions to talking about yesterday.

는 adds contrastive nuance: having talked about the trip overall, she shifts focus to yesterday specifically. The sentence is left incomplete — a very natural trailing-off pattern in spoken Korean as the speaker collects their thoughts.

grammar.meaning: Comparative particle — 'like, as, similar to'
Emphasized inability — 'as for doing X, couldn't'
Connects two clauses — 'and / and then'
Converts an adjective into an adverb — 'in a … way'
Indicates 'at the time of / when' — a temporal noun modifier

sentences.en: What did I do yesterday?
sentences.fr: Qu'ai-je fait hier ?

words.notes: 반말 first-person pronoun. The formal equivalent is 저. Hwasa uses 나 throughout, consistent with the intimate fan-talk register on BStage.
Functions as a time adverb here. No particle needed — time nouns like 어제, 오늘, 내일 can function adverbially without 에.
Colloquial contraction of 무엇 ('what'). Extremely common in spoken Korean. Can also be used as a filler word ('well…'). Here it's a genuine question word.

~(았/었)냐 is a casual (해라체) past-tense question ending. More blunt/casual than ~(았/었)어? Here Hwasa is asking herself aloud — a self-directed rhetorical question as she tries to remember what she did yesterday. This 'thinking out loud' style is very natural in Korean live streams.

grammar.meaning: Blunt/casual past tense question ending — 'did …?'
Asks 'what' as the object of the verb

sentences.en: yesterday
sentences.fr: hier

words.notes: Hwasa is repeating the word as she thinks aloud, trying to recall what she did. This kind of repetition and trailing off is extremely common in natural spoken Korean, especially during live streams. A single-word utterance functioning as a self-directed prompt.

sentences.en: yesterday
sentences.fr: hier

words.notes: Now she adds the topic particle 는, setting up 'yesterday' as the topic she's about to say something about. The contrast with sentence 96 (bare 어제) nicely illustrates how Korean speakers build up their utterances incrementally in real time. The 는 signals she's ready to make a statement about yesterday specifically, likely contrasting it with the overall trip. The sentence remains incomplete — she's still gathering her thoughts.

grammar.meaning: Sets up a topic that the speaker is about to comment on — 'as for X…'

sentences.ko: 와서 짐 풀고 뭐하고 하다가 리허설 하러 갔다가 하니까 깜깜해져 있었는데 방에 와서 책 좀 읽다가 운동하고
sentences.en: I came and unpacked and did something, then went to rehearsal and it was dark, so I came to my room and read a book and then worked out.
sentences.fr: Je suis venu, j'ai défait mes bagages et j'ai fait quelque chose, puis je suis allé à la répétition et il faisait noir, alors je suis venu dans ma chambre et j'ai lu un livre, puis je me suis entraîné.

words.notes: 오 + 아서 contracts to 와서. ~아/어서 indicates sequential actions ('did X and then did Y') or cause/reason. Here it's sequential: 'arrived and then…' The subject (나) is omitted, as is very common in Korean when context makes it clear. 오다 is irregular: 오 + 아 → 와.
Native Korean word for luggage/load. Here the object particle 을 is dropped — extremely common in casual spoken Korean. Full form would be 짐을 풀고.

words.root: 풀다 (to untie, to unpack, to solve)
words.notes: 짐을 풀다 = 'to unpack luggage' (literally 'to untie/release luggage'). ~고 connects actions in sequence. 풀다 has many meanings: untie, solve (a problem), release (tension), unpack — context determines which.

words.breakdown: 뭐 (what/something) + 하 (하다, to do) + 고 (connective ending)
words.definition: did this and that, did whatever
words.notes: 뭐하다 here is used vaguely to mean 'did stuff / did whatever' — a filler when the speaker doesn't want to enumerate every action. Very natural in casual spoken Korean for glossing over minor details.

words.definition: was doing (stuff) and then, in the middle of doing (things)
words.notes: ~다가 indicates that one action was interrupted or transitioned into another: 'was doing X, and then (switched to) Y.' Here: 'was doing this and that, and then (went to rehearsal).' This is a key intermediate grammar pattern for narrating sequences of events.

Konglish loanword from English 'rehearsal.' Pronounced 리허설 [ri-heo-seol]. Very commonly used in the Korean entertainment industry. Hwasa is referring to her rehearsal for the Hong Kong FWD Champions Day performance.

words.definition: in order to do, to go do
words.notes: ~(으)러 expresses purpose and is specifically used with verbs of movement (가다, 오다, 다니다). 리허설 하러 갔다가 = 'went (in order) to do a rehearsal.' Cannot be used with non-movement verbs.

words.definition: went and then (came back / moved on to something else)
words.notes: ~았/었다가 indicates a completed action followed by a change or reversal: 'went (there), and then (something else happened / came back).' Subtly different from bare ~다가 — the past tense marker 았 emphasizes the action was completed before the transition. 갔다가 often implies a round trip or that the going was temporary.

words.definition: and when (I did that) / so, because of doing that
words.notes: ~(으)니까 expresses cause/reason or temporal discovery ('when I did X, I found that Y'). Here it has the discovery nuance: 'when I did all that (went to rehearsal and came back), (I found that) it had gotten dark.' This 'upon doing X, discovered Y' usage is a key intermediate pattern.

words.breakdown: 깜깜하 + 여 (해, connective) + 지 (지다, to become) + 어 (connective)
words.notes: 깜깜하다 is an onomatopoeic/mimetic (의태어) adjective meaning 'pitch dark.' ~아/어지다 means 'to become (a state)': 깜깜해지다 = 'to become dark.' The form 깜깜해져 is the ~아/어 connective form of 깜깜해지다. This Adj + 지다 pattern is essential for expressing changes of state.

words.definition: it was (in that state), and… / it had become dark, but…
words.notes: 깜깜해져 있었는데: the ~아/어 있다 pattern indicates a resultant state ('was in the state of having become dark'). ~는데 provides background information before the next clause: 'it was dark, and so / given that…' The full chain 깜깜해져 있었는데 = 'it had gotten dark (and in that context)…'

words.definition: to the room, in the room
words.notes: 에 here indicates direction/destination ('to the room'). Likely referring to her hotel room in Hong Kong.
Object particle 을 is dropped in casual speech. Full form: 책을 읽다.
Contraction of 조금 ('a little'). Very frequent in spoken Korean. Can soften a statement ('read a bit') or make requests more polite. Here it's casual hedging: 'read a little.'

words.definition: was reading and then (switched to something else)
words.notes: ~다가 again indicating a transition: 'was reading, and then (switched to working out).' Note 읽 has a complex final consonant cluster ㄺ — pronounced [일] before consonants, [읽] before vowels.

words.breakdown: 운동 (運動, exercise) + 하 (하다, to do) + 고 (connective ending)
words.notes: 운동 is Sino-Korean: 운(運) = move + 동(動) = motion. 운동하다 = 'to exercise/work out.' ~고 connects to the next sentence (99), which continues the narrative. The sentence trails off — a natural feature of spoken Korean storytelling.

grammar.meaning: Indicates sequence ('did X and then Y') or cause ('because X, Y')
Indicates one action was interrupted or transitioned into another — 'was doing X, then Y'
Expresses purpose with a movement verb — 'go/come in order to do X'
Did X (completely) and then changed/reversed — often implies a round trip or shift
Because / when (I did X, I discovered Y)
To become (a certain state) — converts adjective into a process verb
To be in the state of having done X — focuses on the resulting condition
Provides background context or mild contrast before the next clause — 'and so / but / given that'
Connects actions in sequence — 'and / and then'

sentences.en: I said it was about two or three in the morning.
sentences.fr: J'ai dit qu'il était environ deux ou trois heures du matin.

words.notes: ~았/었더니 is used when the speaker performed an action in the past, and then discovered an unexpected or notable result. Here: 'After doing all that (reading, working out — continued from sentence 98), I found that it was already 2-3 AM.' The subject of the first clause must be the speaker (first person) when expressing personal discovery. This is an advanced retrospective grammar pattern.

words.definition: the early morning hours, dawn, the wee hours
words.notes: 새벽 refers to the period roughly from midnight to sunrise (approximately 1 AM–5 AM). It's distinct from 아침 (morning). 새벽 두세시 = 'two or three o'clock in the early morning.'
Colloquial approximation marker, similar to 약 (Sino-Korean) or 대략. Placed directly before the number/quantity it modifies. Very common in spoken Korean: 한 두세시 = 'about two or three o'clock.'

words.breakdown: 두 (native Korean 2) + 세 (native Korean 3) + 시 (時, hour/o'clock)
words.notes: Korean has a pattern of combining two consecutive native numbers to express an approximate range: 두세 = 'two or three.' Other examples: 서너 (three or four), 대여섯 (five or six). 시 is the Sino-Korean counter for clock hours. Note: telling time uses native Korean numbers for the hour (한시, 두시, 세시…) and Sino-Korean numbers for minutes.

words.definition: it turned out that…, I noticed/realized that…
words.notes: ~더라고(요) is a retrospective sentence ending used to report something the speaker personally witnessed or experienced in the past. It conveys 'I noticed/realized/found that…' Here: 'it turned out to be about 2-3 AM.' The 고 at the end is a softening particle (technically quotative), making it slightly less blunt than ~더라. Without 요, it's 반말. This is one of the most characteristically Korean endings — it has no direct English equivalent and is a hallmark of natural spoken Korean narration.

grammar.meaning: After (I) did X, (I) discovered/found that Y — the speaker's past action led to an unexpected finding
Reports something the speaker personally experienced or noticed — 'it turned out that… / I realized that…'
Approximately, about — placed before a number to indicate an estimate
Two consecutive native numbers combined to express 'X or Y' as an approximate range

sentences.en: Come back around two or three o'clock
sentences.fr: Revenez vers deux ou trois heures

words.breakdown: 두 (native Korean 2) + 세 (native Korean 3) + 시 (時, hour/o'clock)
words.notes: Same approximate number pair as in sentence 99. Combines two consecutive native Korean numbers to indicate an approximate range. Hwasa is continuing her story from the previous sentences — she's describing coming back to her room around 2-3 AM.

Attaches directly after a noun or number to mean 'approximately / around.' 두세시쯤 = 'around two or three o'clock.' Similar in meaning to 한 (placed before the number) or 정도 (placed after), but 쯤 is the most colloquial of the three. Can also be used with non-numerical nouns: 나쯤 = 'someone like me.'
Indicates repetition of an action. Here: she came back to the room again (having left for rehearsal, exercise, etc. earlier). Very common and essential adverb.

Same contraction as sentence 98: 오 + 아서 → 와서. Sequential meaning: 'came back and then (did something).' The sentence trails off — Hwasa is narrating in a stream-of-consciousness style and either gets interrupted by a fan comment (sentence 101) or pauses to think.

grammar.meaning: Approximately, around — attaches after nouns/numbers to indicate an estimate
Did X and then Y — connects sequential actions

sentences.ko: 인터넷 쇼핑이 좋냐고 직접 보고 사는 게 좋냐고
sentences.en: Is it better to shop online or see it in person?
sentences.fr: Est-il préférable d'acheter en ligne ou de le voir en personne ?

words.notes: Konglish loanword from English 'internet.' Used here as a modifier for 쇼핑: 인터넷 쇼핑 = 'online shopping / internet shopping.'
Konglish loanword from English 'shopping.' 이 is the subject particle after consonant-ending nouns. 인터넷 쇼핑이 좋다 = 'online shopping is good/better.'

words.breakdown: 좋 + 으냐 (plain interrogative for adjectives) + 고 (quotation particle)
words.notes: Indirect quotation of a question: Adj stem + (으)냐고. Hwasa is reading aloud or paraphrasing a fan's question from the live chat. The ~냐고 pattern quotes someone else's question. For adjectives: stem + (으)냐고. For action verbs: stem + 느냐고 or 냐고.
Sino-Korean word: 직(直) = straight/direct + 접(接) = contact. Used as an adverb here: 직접 보고 사다 = 'to see in person and buy.' Contrasts with 인터넷 쇼핑 (online shopping).
~고 connects two sequential actions: 'see it and (then) buy it.' 보다 has a wide range of meanings (see, watch, look at, try, take an exam, etc.).

~는 is the present tense adnominal (modifier) ending for action verbs. 사는 modifies 게 (것이): '(the act of) buying.' 직접 보고 사는 게 = 'the thing of seeing in person and buying' = 'buying after seeing in person.'

words.definition: the thing (of doing something), the act (of)
words.notes: 게 is a spoken contraction of 것이. 것 is a bound noun meaning 'thing/fact.' Here 사는 게 좋다 = 'buying (in person) is good/better.' The contraction 게 (= 것이) is extremely common in spoken Korean. Written/formal form: 것이.

grammar.meaning: Quotes someone else's question — '(someone) asks whether / is asking if'
It is good/better to do X — nominalizes a verb clause for evaluation
Presents two alternatives as quoted questions — 'asking whether A or whether B'
grammar.example_in_sentence: 인터넷 쇼핑이 좋냐고 직접 보고 사는 게 좋냐고

grammar.meaning: Spoken contraction of the nominalizer 것 + subject particle 이

sentences.en: yes
sentences.fr: Oui

words.notes: Polite/neutral affirmative response. Can also function as a filler/acknowledgment ('uh-huh') in conversation. Here Hwasa is likely acknowledging a fan's comment in the live chat before continuing. Other variants: 예 (slightly more formal), 응/어 (반말). 네 is appropriate across most speech levels and is the safest 'yes' for learners.

grammar.meaning: Yes / acknowledgment — used across speech levels as a neutral affirmative

sentences.ko: 저녁은 아 가게 이름이 생각이 안 난다
sentences.en: For dinner, I can't remember the name of the store.
sentences.fr: Pour le dîner, je ne me souviens plus du nom du magasin.

words.notes: 저녁 can mean both 'evening' (time) and 'dinner' (meal). 은 marks it as the topic of the sentence. Hwasa starts to talk about dinner but then gets sidetracked trying to remember the restaurant name — a very natural spoken pattern.

words.definition: ah, oh — expressing frustration or trying to recall something
words.notes: Here 아 signals a mental interruption — Hwasa realizes mid-sentence that she can't remember the name. Different intonation from the 아 of realization in sentence 91; here it's more of a frustrated 'ugh' or 'hmm.'

가게 literally means 'store/shop' but is often used colloquially to refer to restaurants/eateries as well, especially smaller or casual ones. Derived from 가다 (to go) — historically a place one 'goes to.'
이 is the subject particle after consonant-ending nouns. 가게 이름이 = 'the store's name.' Note that Korean often omits possessive markers (의) in casual speech: 가게 이름 rather than 가게의 이름.

In the fixed expression 생각이 나다 ('a thought comes/arises'), 생각 is the subject — the thought 'comes to' the speaker. This is different from English where 'I remember' has the person as subject. Korean conceptualizes remembering as the memory arising on its own.
Short-form negation. 안 나다 = 'does not come (to mind).' 생각이 안 나다 = 'can't remember / the thought doesn't come.'

words.root: 나다 (to come out, to arise, to occur)
words.breakdown: 나 + ㄴ다 (plain present declarative ending for action verbs)
words.notes: 나다 means 'to come out / to arise / to occur.' In 생각이 나다 it means 'to come to mind / to remember.' The ending ~ㄴ다 is the 해라체 (plain) present tense for action verbs — Hwasa is speaking/thinking aloud to herself. This self-directed plain style is very natural when narrating one's own thoughts on a live stream.

grammar.pattern: 생각이 나다 / 생각이 안 나다 (fixed expression)
grammar.meaning: To remember / to not be able to remember — literally 'a thought arises / doesn't arise'
Negates the following verb — 'not / doesn't'
Plain-level present tense statement — used in self-talk, diary writing, narration
Sets up a topic that the speaker abandons or redirects mid-sentence — natural in spoken Korean

sentences.ko: 아 가게 이름이 생각이 안 난다
sentences.en: Oh, I can't remember the name of the store.
sentences.fr: Oh, je ne me souviens plus du nom du magasin.

words.definition: oh, ah — expressing continued frustration at not remembering
words.notes: Hwasa repeats the same phrase from sentence 103 (minus 저녁은), emphasizing her frustration. Repetition for emphasis or while struggling to recall something is very natural in spoken Korean.
Same as sentence 103. Refers to the restaurant she went to for dinner in Hong Kong.

Same structure as 103. Subject of the expression 생각이 안 나다. Note the double-subject construction: 가게 이름이 생각이 안 난다 — 'the store's name, the memory doesn't come' — with both 이름이 and 생각이 marked as subjects. This multiple-subject pattern is characteristic of Korean.
Part of the fixed expression 생각이 나다. The double-subject construction (이름이 생각이) is a key feature of Korean grammar that has no direct parallel in English or French.
Short-form negation before 나다.

Same form as 103. 해라체 self-talk register. The repetition of the entire phrase across two consecutive sentences perfectly captures the natural rhythm of someone struggling to recall information during a live broadcast.
